UNIT.subject: Biology
UNIT.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.3: Excretion and Homeostasis in Animals
UNIT.content:
• Excretory structures and products in animals (insects, birds, freshwater and marine fish)
• Internal structure of the mammalian kidney (cortex, medulla, pelvis, structure and function of the nephron)
• Process of urine formation in mammals
• Internal structure of the mammalian skin
• Role of the liver and skin in excretion
• Homeostatic regulation in humans (osmoregulation, thermoregulation, blood sugar regulation, including diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus)
• Liver diseases and disorders (cirrhosis, hepatitis, fatty liver disease)
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) Relate excretory structures to their products in animals (insects, birds, freshwater and marine fish).
b) Relate the internal structure of the mammalian kidney to its function.
c) Describe the process of urine formation in mammals.
d) Relate the structure of the mammalian liver and skin to their excretory functions.
e) Illustrate homeostatic regulation in humans.
f) Reflect on the importance of excretion and homeostasis in animals.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: The learner asks questions to be clear on what they need while discussing how animals in the locality respond to changes in the environment (Lesson 6: basking, panting, burrowing, hibernation, aestivation).
• Digital Literacy: The learner uses digital technology effectively while using digital devices to watch animations on the process of urine formation in mammals (Lesson 3, with shared group viewing).
• Communication and Collaboration: Learners work in peer groups to dissect, model, label and present the internal structures of the mammalian kidney (Lesson 2).
UNIT.values:
• Social Justice: The learner shares resources equitably while modelling and labelling the internal structure of a mammalian kidney, including fair sharing of dissecting tools and modelling materials.
• Responsibility: The learner engages in assigned roles and duties while dissecting a mammalian kidney to observe the internal structure.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions: Learners add questions to the Driving Question Board (DQB) after observing the dog, lizard, goat and fish, and refine them as each lesson adds evidence.
• Developing and Using Models: Learners draw and label a kidney, build a clay/chart nephron model, and build flowcharts, then revise one cumulative explanatory model each lesson.
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: Learners dissect a fresh kidney from a local butchery and record observations safely.
• Analyzing and Interpreting Data: Learners compare nitrogenous wastes across animals, trace fluid composition along the nephron, and interpret diabetes case-study data.
• Constructing Explanations: Learners explain why animals differ in how they lose heat, water and wastes using structure-function evidence.
• Engaging in Argument from Evidence: Learners challenge misconceptions, such as sweating being only for waste removal, using evidence.
• Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information: Learners use charts, animations, photomicrographs and a resource person, then present findings to peers.
UNIT.pcis:
• Environmental Conservation: The learner observes laboratory safety while dissecting the mammalian kidney to observe internal structure, including proper biohazard disposal of specimens.
• Waste Management: The learner appreciated the need to conserve biodiversity while observing and discussing how animals in the locality respond to changes in the environment.
• Health Education: Learners explore liver disorders (cirrhosis, hepatitis, fatty liver disease) and metabolic disorders (diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus) and discuss prevention and management (Lessons 4 and 5).
UNIT.careers:
• Veterinary Medicine: Understanding how livestock such as goats and dogs regulate water, heat and wastes.
• Human Medicine and Nursing: Diagnosing and managing kidney disease, liver disease and diabetes.
• Medical Pathology and Laboratory Technology: Examining tissue structure of kidney, liver and skin.
• Physiological Research: Studying feedback mechanisms and adaptations to stress.
• Environmental Conservation and Wildlife Management: Understanding how wild animals in Kenya's Rift Valley, Tsavo and Lake Victoria cope with heat, drought and changing conditions.
UNIT.focus: This unit uses one everyday Kenyan puzzle, a panting dog, a motionless lizard, goats producing concentrated urine and freshwater fish producing dilute urine, to drive learning about excretion and homeostasis. Learners predict, gather evidence through charts, a kidney dissection, animations and case studies, and make sense of it through negative feedback ideas. They revise one cumulative model and track growing understanding on the DQB, using locally available materials and shared digital devices.
UNIT.phenomenon: On a hot afternoon in a local community, a dog pants rapidly with its tongue hanging out, while a lizard sits motionless on a warm rock. Nearby, goats drink water yet produce concentrated urine, whereas local freshwater fish continually excrete large amounts of dilute urine. All these animals face the same environment and the same need to get rid of wastes and keep the body stable, yet each behaves very differently. Students must ask why a hot lizard stays still on a hot rock, why a dog pants, why goats and fish handle water so differently, and how each animal keeps its internal conditions steady and removes toxic wastes.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A person who has run in the sun (such as a athlete training in Iten) sweats, turns red and feels thirsty, but passes little, dark urine.
• Birds and insects excrete a whitish, semi-solid paste instead of liquid urine, while marine fish live in salty water yet do not dehydrate.
• A person with untreated diabetes mellitus is constantly thirsty, passes a lot of urine and has sugar in the blood, which suggests that body regulation has failed.
• Animals in Kenya's dry areas burrow, aestivate or hibernate during extreme weather, and survive by reducing activity and water loss.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How do different animals maintain a balanced internal environment and eliminate toxic wastes despite drastic changes in their external conditions?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How do animals get rid of waste products?
2. How do animals cope with environmental changes?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: Insects, birds, freshwater fish and marine fish have specialized excretory structures adapted to eliminate specific nitrogenous wastes (uric acid, ammonia, urea) based on water availability. Learners explore charts and reference texts to compare excretory organs and products. Leads to: How do mammals (like humans) process and filter their internal liquid wastes?
Lesson 2: The mammalian kidney contains distinct regions (cortex, medulla, pelvis) and functional units (nephrons) designed for blood filtration. Learners dissect a locally obtained kidney (from a butchery), draw the internal structures and build and label a model with peers, following safety and biohazard disposal procedures. Leads to: How exactly does the nephron turn filtered blood into urine?
Lesson 3: Urine formation involves ultrafiltration in the glomerulus followed by selective reabsorption and secretion in the nephron tubule. Groups watch animations on shared devices and trace changes in fluid composition. Leads to: What other organs in mammals assist in excretion besides the kidney?
Lesson 4: The skin and liver possess specialized structures that eliminate metabolic wastes and process toxic substances. Learners observe photomicrographs and illustrations and discuss deamination, bile production and sweat secretion, and hear from a resource person on liver disorders (cirrhosis, hepatitis, fatty liver disease). Leads to: How does the body keep internal water, temperature and sugar levels constant during external changes?
Lesson 5: The body uses negative feedback control to regulate water levels (osmoregulation, ADH) and blood glucose (insulin and glucagon). Learners construct feedback flowcharts and evaluate case studies of diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus. Leads to: How does the body keep core temperature stable when the outside weather changes drastically?
Lesson 6: Thermoregulation involves physiological mechanisms (sweating, vasodilation, vasoconstriction) and behavioral adjustments to control body heat. Learners analyze feedback loops and discuss local animal behaviors (basking, panting, burrowing, hibernation, aestivation), explaining the dog and lizard in the anchoring phenomenon. Leads to: Why are excretion and homeostasis so vital for the overall survival of living organisms?
Lesson 7: Maintaining a constant internal environment (homeostasis) and clearing metabolic waste (excretion) are essential for cellular survival and overall health. Learners synthesize evidence into a final explanatory model, reflect on the importance of excretion and homeostasis, and present solutions to DQB questions. Unit reflection (no further question).

LESSONS.title: Same Hot Afternoon, Different Bodies: Launching the Excretion and Homeostasis Puzzle
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.3: Excretion and Homeostasis in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: excretion, homeostasis, nitrogenous waste, ammonia, urea, uric acid, osmoregulation, thermoregulation, Malpighian tubules, gills, kidney, panting, basking

slo.purpose: To launch the anchoring phenomenon (a panting dog, a still lizard, goats producing concentrated urine and freshwater fish producing dilute urine on the same hot afternoon) and help learners compare the excretory structures and nitrogenous products of insects, birds, freshwater fish and marine fish in relation to water availability.
slo.knowledge: Learners relate excretory structures and products in animals (insects, birds, freshwater and marine fish): ammonia (freshwater fish, via gills and dilute urine), urea (marine cartilaginous fish and mammals), uric acid (insects via Malpighian tubules, and birds via kidneys). Learners recognise that the form of nitrogenous waste depends on water availability.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (initial mental model of how an animal keeps its body stable and removes waste); asking questions (sticky notes for the DQB); analysing and interpreting data from charts and reference texts; constructing explanations; communicating with peers (Think-Pair-Share).
slo.attitudes: Core competency: Critical Thinking and Problem Solving, as learners ask questions to be clear on what they need while discussing how animals in the locality respond to changes in the environment. Value: Responsibility, as learners take on assigned group roles. PCI: Environmental Conservation, as learners appreciate the need to conserve biodiversity while observing and discussing how animals in the locality respond to environmental changes.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do animals get rid of waste products? 2. How do animals cope with environmental changes?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the opening lesson. It surfaces learners' ideas about waste removal and body stability, sets up the Driving Question Board, and builds the comparative base (waste products linked to water availability across insects, birds and fish). It ends with the question: How do mammals (like humans) process and filter their internal liquid wastes? That leads to Lesson 2 on the mammalian kidney.
slo.safetyNotes: This lesson uses no live animals or dissection. If learners observe animals outdoors, they must keep a safe distance and not touch dogs, lizards or livestock. Learners wash hands after handling shared charts and materials. Make sure no learner is left standing in direct sun during the outdoor-observation talk. No kidney dissection happens in this lesson; dissection safety (gloves, aprons, sharp-tool rules, handwashing) will be taught before the later dissection lesson.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin with the puzzle of a hot afternoon in a Kenyan community: a dog pants, a lizard sits still on a warm rock, goats drink water yet produce concentrated urine, and freshwater fish excrete large volumes of dilute urine. Learners first draw an initial model of how one animal (dog, lizard or human) handles excess heat or waste, and share their ideas in pairs. They then use charts and reference texts, working in groups of 4-6 with shared copies, to compare excretory organs and nitrogenous wastes (ammonia, urea, uric acid) in insects, birds, freshwater fish and marine fish, and connect these to water availability. In the explain phase they use the evidence to revise their thinking about the fish and goat part of the puzzle. The class then launches the Driving Question Board with sticky-note questions, and finally makes a first class model that shows what they know and what is still unexplained, leading to the next question: How do mammals (like humans) process and filter their internal liquid wastes?

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the phenomenon (teacher reads the scenario aloud and sketches the four animals on the board, or shows a poster): a dog panting, a lizard still on a hot rock, goats drinking yet producing concentrated urine, and freshwater fish excreting large amounts of dilute urine near Lake Victoria or a local dam. Individually (4 minutes), each learner draws an initial mental model/diagram showing how ONE animal (dog, lizard or human) handles excess heat or internal waste, using arrows and labels, and writes a one-sentence prediction: 'I think the dog pants because...'. Learners then Think-Pair-Share with a neighbour (3 minutes) and add or change one thing in their drawing using a different colour pen.
framework.teacherMoves: Read the scenario slowly, then say: 'Same hot afternoon, same village, same need to stay stable and get rid of wastes. Why do these animals behave so differently?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking any answer. Say: 'Draw what you think is happening INSIDE the animal. There are no wrong drawings today; I want your honest first thinking.' Circulate and look for ideas about sweat, water loss, heat, urine and wastes without correcting. Ask 2-3 learners at each desk cluster: 'What does your arrow show?' During the share, cold-call 4 pairs from different parts of the room (not volunteers only): 'Tell us what your partner added to the drawing.' Record recurring ideas on the board under 'Our first ideas' (e.g., 'panting cools the body', 'fish have too much water', 'lizard saves energy'). Do not confirm or correct. Collect drawings later and keep them in a folder for the Model Building phase and the end-of-unit comparison. For large classes, have back-row learners share with a pair behind them, then take answers from each row.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share, with an initial model drawing. Individual thinking first gives every learner time to put their own ideas on paper, and pair talk lets them test and refine ideas in a low-risk setting. The drawn initial model makes hidden preconceptions visible (e.g., 'waste is just sweat' or 'all animals urinate the same way') so they can be revisited and revised later in the storyline.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Learner's drawing includes at least one label for heat, water or waste and an arrow showing movement or loss. (2) Learner can state a prediction using 'I think... because...'. (3) Learner adds or changes at least one idea after the pair talk (different colour). Note common ideas and misconceptions (e.g., 'only mammals excrete', 'sweating is the only way to lose waste', 'fish do not urinate') on a quick tally sheet. Oral probe: 'What made you draw that arrow?'

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 4-6 (with assigned roles: reader, recorder, chart-keeper, reporter), learners explore the charts and reference texts on excretory structures in insects, birds, freshwater fish and marine fish, one set per group. Using a comparison table (Animal | Excretory organ/structure | Main nitrogenous waste | Water used to remove waste (a lot/some/very little) | Habitat/water availability), they record evidence, e.g., freshwater fish (e.g., tilapia from Lake Victoria): gills and kidneys, ammonia, lots of dilute urine; marine fish: gills with chloride cells, kidneys, urea/trimethylamine oxide in cartilaginous fish, very little concentrated urine; insects (e.g., locust, housefly): Malpighian tubules, uric acid, almost solid paste; birds (e.g., chicken, ostrich, flamingo at Lake Nakuru): kidneys, uric acid, white paste in droppings. Groups then answer two guiding questions: 'Which animals need to save water, and what waste do they make?' and 'Which animals have plenty of water, and what waste do they make?' Groups share a few shared charts, rotating every 8 minutes if materials are limited.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute charts/reference texts, one set per group, and display one chart at the front for the whole class. Say: 'You are scientists comparing evidence. Look for patterns between where an animal lives and the waste it makes.' Model the first row of the table on the board using the freshwater fish. Set a timer for 20 minutes. Circulate with a checklist; ask: 'Which column shows how much water this animal can spare?' and 'What do you notice about the animals that make uric acid?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each probe. Ensure every learner has a role and that the quietest learner reads or records at least once; cold-call 3 groups to report one row of their table. Prompt for evidence: 'Which chart or sentence tells you that?' Redirect misconceptions gently: 'Check the text again, what does it say about water use?' For groups finishing early, ask them to extend their table by adding the lizard and the goat from the phenomenon and to make a prediction about their waste.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured evidence comparison using a data table (a pattern-finding strategy). Organising the same categories across different animals makes patterns visible: less water available means a less toxic, less soluble waste (uric acid), while plenty of water means ammonia can be flushed away. Group roles and shared materials support equitable participation in large classes.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Group table has all four animal groups filled in with organ and nitrogenous waste. (2) Learners correctly pair ammonia with freshwater fish, urea with marine cartilaginous fish, and uric acid with insects and birds. (3) Learners cite chart or text evidence when explaining. (4) Each learner can name their role and what they contributed. Teacher uses an oral probe at each group: 'Show me the line in the text that supports your column.' Record groups needing support.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to individual thinking first: they write 2-3 sentences answering 'Why do freshwater fish excrete lots of dilute urine and ammonia, while insects and birds excrete a semi-solid uric acid paste?' using at least two pieces of evidence from their tables. They then Think-Pair-Share and join another pair to build a four-person explanation. Next the class discusses the phenomenon: 'What does this tell us about the goat and the freshwater fish?' Learners use their data to explain that fish living in water take in water by osmosis and must remove it as dilute urine, while terrestrial animals conserve water. They also name what is still NOT explained: how the goat produces concentrated urine, why the dog pants, and why the lizard sits on a hot rock. Learners add a 'Now I think...' box to their initial model drawing in a different colour.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use your evidence. Complete this sentence: Animals that have little water make ___ because ___.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then allow pairs to talk for 2 minutes. Cold-call 5 learners across the room to share, asking each: 'What evidence supports that?' and then 'Who can add to or challenge that idea?' Draw a simple line on the board from 'Plenty of water' (ammonia) to 'Very little water' (uric acid), and ask learners to place the animals on it. Link back: 'Now look at the goat and the fish from our hot afternoon. What can we say about each, and what can we NOT yet explain?' Record on a chart under 'What we can explain' and 'What we still cannot explain.' Highlight that the goat's concentrated urine and the dog's panting need something we have not yet studied. Avoid giving the mammalian kidney explanation; say: 'Hold that thought; it will be our next investigation.' Clarify vocabulary (excretion vs egestion; ammonia, urea, uric acid) briefly with a Kenyan example (e.g., white part in chicken droppings is uric acid).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning through Think-Pair-Share and a class discussion. Learners state a claim about waste type and water availability, support it with chart evidence, and reason about why. Naming what remains unexplained builds a productive 'need to know' that drives the next lessons and connects the evidence back to the full phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Written explanation includes a claim, at least two pieces of evidence, and a link to water availability. (2) Learner uses the terms ammonia, urea and uric acid correctly. (3) Learner identifies at least one unexplained part of the phenomenon (goat urine, panting, lizard basking). (4) Learner revises the drawing with a 'Now I think...' note. Oral probe: 'Why would a bird not be able to make dilute ammonia urine like a tilapia?' Quick scan: 3-point check (claim, evidence, reasoning).

framework.learnerExperience: The class reads the Driving Question aloud: 'How do different animals maintain a balanced internal environment and eliminate toxic wastes despite drastic changes in their external conditions?' Individually, each learner writes 2 questions on sticky notes about the phenomenon (e.g., 'Why does a dog pant instead of sweat?', 'How do goats make concentrated urine?', 'Why does a lizard bask on a hot rock?', 'How do human kidneys clean blood?'). Learners place notes on the DQB, grouped under categories that emerge (Waste removal, Water balance, Temperature control, Body organs). Learners vote on 2-3 priority questions to investigate next, and a group volunteers to be 'DQB keepers' for the week.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Driving Question on a large chart at the front. Say: 'Write questions you really want answered, questions that start with how or why.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before they begin writing. Model one good question and one weaker one ('What is urine?' vs 'Why does goat urine look darker than fish urine?'). Collect sticky notes row by row so that every learner contributes. Cold-call 4 learners to read and place their question, asking: 'Which part of the phenomenon does your question come from?' Cluster notes with the class: 'Which notes belong together? What should we call this group?' Connect to the KICD key inquiry questions: 'How do animals get rid of waste products? How do animals cope with environmental changes?' and place both on the board. Point out the question 'How do mammals (like humans) process and filter their internal liquid wastes?' (add it if no learner raises it) and link it to the goat. If wall space is limited, use a large manila sheet or a section of the chalkboard and photograph it. Assign DQB keepers.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board discussion. The DQB makes learners' curiosity visible and gives them ownership of the investigation sequence. Clustering questions helps them see relationships among excretion, osmoregulation and thermoregulation, and the board is revisited after each lesson to track growing understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each learner submits at least two questions. (2) At least some questions are testable or explanatory (how/why) rather than simple recall. (3) Learners can say which part of the phenomenon their question comes from. (4) Learners participate in sorting and voting. Teacher records the number of 'how/why' questions and notes learners who need support in question-writing. Oral probe: 'What would you need to find out to answer that?'

framework.learnerExperience: In their groups, learners build a first class/group model on a manila sheet or in their notebooks: a labelled diagram showing the four animals from the phenomenon (dog, lizard, goat, freshwater fish) and, for each, what they think is happening to heat, water and waste inside the body. Using what they learned in this lesson, they add the nitrogenous waste and the excretory organs for fish, insects and birds, and use a different colour or question marks (?) for parts they cannot yet explain (goat's kidney, dog's panting, lizard's basking). Groups do a gallery walk (5 minutes) to compare models, leaving one 'I like/I wonder' note on another group's model. Finally, each learner completes an exit ticket.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'This is our first model. It will change as we learn more. Show what you know in one colour, and mark what you do not yet know with question marks.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after setting the task. Provide one sheet of manila paper and markers per group; where materials are limited, allow notebook drawings. Circulate and ask: 'Where does the waste leave the body in this animal?' and 'What happens to water in this part of your model?' During the gallery walk, cold-call 3 learners to share one thing they noticed in another group's model. Close by linking to Lesson 2: 'We can explain fish, insects and birds, but the goat's urine and the human body leave us with a big question: How do mammals (like humans) process and filter their internal liquid wastes? Next lesson we will start finding out.' Hand out exit tickets: (1) One thing I now understand about nitrogenous wastes and water. (2) One question I still have. (3) Which animal's waste is hardest to explain and why? Collect models and keep them for revision in later lessons. Remind learners to bring any questions about kidneys and ask them to look at a goat or cow kidney at home or at a butchery (observation only, not handling).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model Building and Revision. A first visible model, with unknown parts marked, captures current understanding and shows gaps that need evidence. Gallery walk peer feedback encourages comparison and critique, and the model will be revised at the end of each lesson as the storyline develops.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Model shows all four animals with at least one label of heat, water or waste for each. (2) Model correctly includes the excretory organ and waste for at least two of fish, insect, bird. (3) Model identifies gaps using question marks. (4) Peer feedback uses 'I like/I wonder' appropriately. Exit ticket: learner names one correct fact on nitrogenous wastes and water, and asks one relevant question. Tally exit tickets into 'secure', 'developing' and 'needs support' to plan Lesson 2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners' initial drawings reveal misconceptions (e.g., that all animals urinate in the same way, or that panting is just tiredness) that need targeted evidence later? Did every learner, including quieter ones in a large class, contribute a drawing, a role, and at least two DQB questions? Were charts and reference texts shared fairly among groups, and did rotation work? Which learners could link water availability to the type of nitrogenous waste, and who still needs support? Were the DQB questions mostly recall or genuine how/why questions, and how will you help learners improve them? Did the unexplained parts (goat urine, panting, lizard basking) create real curiosity about the mammalian kidney for Lesson 2? Note which Kenyan examples (tilapia from Lake Victoria, chickens, flamingos at Lake Nakuru, goats) were most engaging, and what you would adjust to manage time and materials next time.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that freshwater fish, marine fish, insects and birds have different excretory structures (gills and kidneys, Malpighian tubules, kidneys) and make different nitrogenous wastes (ammonia, urea, uric acid), and that a dog pants, a lizard sits still on a hot rock, goats produce concentrated urine and freshwater fish produce large amounts of dilute urine.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that the type of nitrogenous waste an animal makes is linked to how much water is available to it: animals with plenty of water (freshwater fish) excrete toxic ammonia in dilute urine, while animals that must save water (insects and birds) excrete less toxic uric acid as a semi-solid paste, and marine cartilaginous fish (such as sharks) and mammals make urea.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that animals living in different environments have excretory structures adapted to remove nitrogenous wastes while conserving or removing water, but we cannot yet explain how a goat makes concentrated urine, why a dog pants, why a lizard basks, or how mammals such as humans filter their internal liquid wastes. That leads us to ask: How do mammals (like humans) process and filter their internal liquid wastes?

LESSONS.title: Inside the Goat Kidney: Cortex, Medulla, Pelvis and Nephrons
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.3: Excretion and Homeostasis in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: kidney, cortex, medulla, renal pelvis, nephron, ureter, renal artery, renal vein, dissection, biohazard, filtration, model

slo.purpose: To help learners discover, through dissection of a locally obtained goat or cow kidney, that the mammalian kidney has distinct regions (cortex, medulla, pelvis) and microscopic functional units (nephrons) designed for blood filtration, and to link this structure to how goats produce concentrated urine while freshwater fish produce dilute urine.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson the learner should be able to: (b) relate the internal structure of the mammalian kidney to its function; identify the cortex, medulla, pelvis, ureter, renal artery and renal vein; state that the nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
slo.skills: Planning and carrying out investigations (dissection), developing and using models (drawing and building a labelled clay/chart model), obtaining, evaluating and communicating information (presenting models to peers), asking questions and defining problems (DQB).
slo.attitudes: Responsibility: engages in assigned roles and duties while dissecting a mammalian kidney. Social Justice: shares resources equitably while modelling and labelling the kidney. Environmental Conservation and Waste Management: observes laboratory safety and disposes of biological waste properly. Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: asks questions to be clear on what they need.
slo.keyInquiry: How do animals get rid of waste products? How do animals cope with environmental changes?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 raised the puzzle of why the dog, lizard, goat and freshwater fish handle water and wastes so differently. Lesson 2 supplies the first structural evidence: the mammalian kidney is built for filtering blood, with regions and nephrons arranged for this job. It leaves learners asking: How exactly does the nephron turn filtered blood into urine? That question drives Lesson 3 (urine formation animation).
slo.safetyNotes: Wear lab coats/aprons, disposable gloves and closed shoes; wash hands with soap and water before and after. Use scalpels only when the teacher permits, cutting away from the body on a tray. Only one trained cutter per group, others observe/record. Kidneys must be fresh, kept cool, and from a licensed butchery. No eating, drinking or touching the face. Dispose of tissue and gloves in a labelled biohazard bag/bin, to be buried in a deep pit or incinerated; disinfect trays and instruments with soapy water/bleach solution. Cover cuts. Keep sharp tools counted before and after.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the hot-afternoon scene of the dog, lizard, goat and fish and predict what the inside of a goat's kidney must look like if it can make concentrated urine. In groups of 4-5 (about 10 groups for a class of 45-50) they dissect a goat or cow kidney from a local butchery, with defined roles, observe cortex, medulla and pelvis, and draw and annotate what they see. They explain how the structure suits blood filtration, then build and label a clay/chart model and peer-review other groups' models. The DQB is updated with new questions, especially about what the nephron does. The class model of how animals maintain a balanced internal environment is revised to include the kidney as the filtering organ.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the phenomenon (panting dog, still lizard, goat producing concentrated urine, freshwater fish producing dilute urine). Individually, in 3 minutes, they sketch what they think the inside of a goat's kidney looks like and write one sentence on how it might help the goat make concentrated urine. They then Think-Pair-Share with a partner, compare sketches and write one prediction on what they expect to see when the kidney is cut open lengthwise (Predict-Observe-Explain, step 1). Time: 12 minutes.
framework.teacherMoves: Display a whole, uncut kidney in a tray (or a picture of one) and ask: "Yesterday we saw that the goat drinks water yet makes concentrated urine. If you could open this organ, what would you expect to see inside?" Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before anyone speaks, then 3 minutes of silent sketching. Circulate and ask 2 pairs: "What part of your sketch would let blood be cleaned?" Cold-call 4 learners from different groups to share predictions and record them on the board under 'Our Predictions'. Do not correct yet; say "Hold that idea, we will test it with evidence in a few minutes."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with Think-Pair-Share. Making predictions first exposes learners' prior ideas (e.g., a kidney is hollow like a bean bag or just a bag of urine) so that the dissection evidence can confirm or challenge them, and pair talk lets every learner rehearse ideas in large classes.
framework.formativeAssessment: Oral probes and sketch check. Look for: sketches showing at least one inner region or tube; predictions mentioning blood supply or filtering; misconceptions such as 'urine is stored inside the kidney'. Tally on a class list how many learners predicted layers versus a hollow structure.

framework.learnerExperience: In assigned roles (cutter, holder/observer, recorder, safety and disposal officer, materials manager) groups put on gloves and aprons and examine the external kidney: the bean shape, fatty capsule, renal artery, renal vein and ureter at the hilum. With the teacher's permission the cutter makes a longitudinal cut from the outer curve to the hilum. Learners observe and note: the darker outer cortex, the paler, striped triangular medulla (pyramids), the funnel-shaped hollow renal pelvis leading to the ureter, and the fine texture of the cortex. They use a hand lens to look for tiny granular dots (renal corpuscles) in the cortex. They draw a labelled, large, pencil drawing of the cut surface, then clean up and dispose of waste in the biohazard bin. Time: 30 minutes.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the dissection give a 3-minute safety briefing: "Gloves on, scalpel always cuts away from you, only the cutter touches the blade, and the safety officer counts the instruments." Demonstrate the first cut on one kidney at the front while groups watch. Ask groups to name roles aloud and rotate roles for the drawing so everyone handles tasks (Responsibility and Social Justice). Circulate with prompts: "Which region is darkest? Which is hollow? Where does the tube leave?" and "What does the colour difference tell you about blood supply?" Cold-call 3 groups to point to the cortex, medulla and pelvis on their specimen. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Supervise disposal: all tissue, gloves and paper towels go into the biohazard bag, and trays are disinfected. With limited kits, let two groups share one dissection kit in turns while the other group drafts the diagram.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (Observe). Direct examination of real tissue provides first-hand evidence that the kidney is organised into distinct regions and a collecting space; drawing forces learners to notice detail and decide what is important.
framework.formativeAssessment: Annotated kidney diagrams plus observation checklist. Indicators: correct labels for cortex, medulla, pelvis, ureter, renal artery, renal vein; accurate relative position (cortex outside, medulla inside, pelvis central); title, scale or magnification note, and neat lines; safe handling observed (gloves on, cutting away from body, correct disposal). Record a tick or comment per group.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups compare their observations with the earlier predictions and discuss: "What did we get right or wrong?" Using a printed or board chart of a nephron (Bowman's capsule, glomerulus, tubule, loop of Henle, collecting duct) the teacher introduces the nephron as the microscopic unit that cannot be seen with the naked eye but is packed in the cortex and medulla. Groups write a claim-evidence-reasoning statement: 'The kidney is suited to filter blood because...' using evidence from their dissection (renal artery brings blood, the cortex contains many filtering units, medulla pyramids collect fluid, the pelvis funnels urine to the ureter). They connect it to the phenomenon, explaining why a goat's kidney, with a well-developed medulla, can produce concentrated urine while a freshwater fish's kidney mainly gets rid of excess water. Time: 18 minutes.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: "Compare your sketch from earlier with what you saw. What surprised you?" WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 4 learners. Introduce the nephron chart: "The cortex looked grainy. Those grains are tiny filters called renal corpuscles, part of each nephron. A goat kidney has about a million of them." Prompt reasoning: "If blood arrives through the renal artery, where must filtering happen, and where would the filtrate leave?" Ask groups to trace the path of fluid with a finger on the diagram from cortex to medulla to pelvis to ureter. Cold-call 3 groups to state the claim and evidence. Correct misconceptions explicitly, e.g., "The pelvis does not make urine; it collects it." Pose the bridging question: "Tissue structure shows where filtering happens, but how is urine actually made?"
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning within Predict-Observe-Explain (Explain). Returning to predictions helps learners revise ideas using evidence and connect structure to function, while the nephron chart links what they saw at the visible scale to the microscopic units.
framework.formativeAssessment: Oral probes and CER statements. Success indicators: learner uses specific dissection evidence (e.g., 'the cortex is dark and granular, showing a rich blood supply') to support a function claim; correctly links pelvis to ureter and urine collection; identifies the nephron as the functional unit. Quick 3-question concept check quiz (1. Name the outer region. 2. Which region collects urine? 3. What is the functional unit?) with a show of fingers or mini-whiteboards.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group writes 2 new questions on sticky notes or paper strips about what they still wonder (for example: How do the nephrons filter blood? Why is the medulla striped? Why does a freshwater fish not need a large medulla? What happens to useful substances like glucose from ugali? How does water loss in panting change urine?). They place the notes on the class DQB under categories (Structure, Process, Different animals, Homeostasis). They cluster similar questions, and mark which earlier questions have now been answered (e.g., 'Which organ filters blood in a goat?'). Time: 8 minutes.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "What new questions has the kidney raised for you?" Allow WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds, then ask each group to submit 2 questions. Cold-call 3 groups to read their questions aloud and place them on the board. Highlight one question: "How exactly does the nephron turn filtered blood into urine?" and say "This is the question we will investigate next lesson using an animation." Put a green tick beside questions answered and ask for the evidence that supports each tick. Photograph the DQB so it can be recreated if the wall space is needed.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board discussion. Learner-generated questions give ownership, show how structure evidence leads to new process questions, and set up a purposeful transition to Lesson 3.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket and DQB quality. Indicators: questions that go beyond naming parts (ask how or why); links to the anchoring phenomenon (dog, lizard, goat, fish); at least one group asking about nephron function. Exit ticket: 'One thing I can now explain about the kidney is ___; one thing I still wonder is ___.'

framework.learnerExperience: Groups use modelling clay, cardboard, manila paper, coloured pencils and string (as vessels) to build and label a 3D or 2D longitudinal section of the kidney showing cortex, medulla (pyramids), pelvis, ureter, renal artery and renal vein, with an inset sketch of a nephron placed in the cortex and medulla. Using a different colour, they add to the class model of homeostasis a box labelled 'Kidney: filters blood and removes nitrogenous waste (urea) and regulates water', linking it to the goat, with a question mark for how the fish differs. Groups conduct a gallery walk: two members stay as presenters while others visit, use a peer-review checklist, and give one 'star' and one 'step' of feedback. Models are revised based on feedback. Time: 12 minutes.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Your model must show where blood enters, where filtering happens, and where urine leaves. Label every part." Ensure equitable sharing of materials (materials manager distributes equally; all members contribute). Circulate asking: "Which part of your model is the filter? How does this relate to the goat's concentrated urine?" WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. For the gallery walk, rotate presenters after 3 minutes and cold-call 3 visiting learners to share a strength they saw. Collect the models and diagrams for display. Remind groups to wash hands, clean up and dispose of materials safely. Preview the next lesson: "We will watch an animation in groups of 5 around one device to see how a nephron makes urine."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model Building & Revision with peer review. Building and labelling a physical model consolidates the structure-function relationship, and revising it after feedback shows that models are improved with evidence; adding the kidney to the class homeostasis model keeps the phenomenon central.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer review of physical models and teacher checklist. Indicators: all six structures correctly labelled; correct relative positions; nephron inset located in cortex/medulla; presenter can explain one structure-function link in a sentence; feedback is specific. Collect annotated diagrams for marking: 4 = all labels correct with function notes; 3 = labels correct; 2 = some errors; 1 = major errors.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Did every learner, not just the cutter, handle the specimen or contribute to the drawing? Which predictions (hollow bag, layers, tubes) were most common and how did the evidence shift them? Were safety and disposal procedures followed without reminders? Which groups confused the pelvis with the medulla or imagined urine being made in the pelvis, and how will I address this at the start of Lesson 3? Were the large-class constraints (shared kits, time) managed without sacrificing quality? Did the DQB questions show curiosity about the nephron and the animals in the opening phenomenon?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed a goat/cow kidney with a dark outer cortex, a paler striped medulla, a hollow renal pelvis leading to the ureter, and blood vessels (renal artery and vein) entering and leaving at the hilum. Granular dots in the cortex suggested tiny filtering units.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The mammalian kidney is organised into regions with different roles: the cortex contains many nephrons where blood is filtered, the medulla contains parts of nephrons and collecting ducts that help concentrate urine, and the pelvis collects urine and passes it to the ureter. The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Because the kidney receives a large blood supply and contains millions of nephrons arranged in the cortex and medulla, it can filter blood, remove urea and regulate water. This helps explain how a goat can drink water yet produce concentrated urine, while we still need to find out how nephrons turn filtered blood into urine and why freshwater fish produce dilute urine.

LESSONS.title: Following the Fluid: How the Nephron Filters Blood and Makes Urine
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.3: Excretion and Homeostasis in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: ultrafiltration, glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, selective reabsorption, secretion, nephron, proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, collecting duct, glucose, urea, ADH, osmoregulation, filtrate, urine

slo.purpose: Learners use digital animations to trace how fluid composition changes along the nephron, so they can explain how a goat produces concentrated urine while a freshwater fish produces large volumes of dilute urine.
slo.knowledge: Describe the process of urine formation in mammals: ultrafiltration in the glomerulus, selective reabsorption in the proximal tubule, loop of Henle and distal tubule, secretion, and water reabsorption in the collecting duct under ADH control. Relate the structure of the nephron to each stage.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (tracing and annotating a nephron flowchart); analysing and interpreting data (comparing fluid composition in blood, filtrate and urine); constructing explanations; using digital devices to gather evidence; asking questions.
slo.attitudes: Responsibility in group roles when sharing a device; Social Justice by sharing devices equitably; curiosity and appreciation of how animals in the locality keep their bodies stable; Digital Literacy through careful use of animations.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do animals get rid of waste products? 2. How do animals cope with environmental changes?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-2 established that excretory structures differ across animals and that the mammalian kidney has a cortex, medulla and pelvis containing nephrons. Lesson 3 explains HOW the nephron makes urine, giving the mechanism behind the goat's concentrated urine. It also raises the gap that the kidney is not the only excretory organ, which leads to Lesson 4 on other organs (liver, skin, lungs).
slo.safetyNotes: Keep devices on stable desks away from water and any kidney specimens; wash hands if kidneys from butcheries were handled earlier in the week; devices are shared, so the Device Manager handles them and cables are kept off walkways; limit screen brightness and sit so all group members can see without crowding.

LESSONS.overview: Students return to the opening scene: the goat drinks water yet produces concentrated urine, while the freshwater fish continually excretes dilute urine. In groups of 6-8 around one shared device, they predict what the kidney does to blood, watch animations of the nephron, and complete a 'Follow the Fluid' table tracing glucose, protein, urea and water in blood, filtrate and urine. They explain why glucose is absent from urine but urea is concentrated, then add the nephron process to the class model and the DQB, ending with the question: what other organs in mammals help with excretion besides the kidney?

framework.learnerExperience: Students recall the goat and fish from the phenomenon and the kidney structure from Lesson 2. Individually they draw a quick sketch or write 2-3 sentences predicting: 'Blood enters the kidney carrying glucose, proteins, urea and water. What do you think comes out as urine, and what happens to the rest?' They then Think-Pair-Share with a neighbour and each pair records one prediction on a sticky note or in the exercise book: 'Urine contains ___ but not ___ because ___.' Groups of 6-8 are formed around the shared device with roles: Device Manager, Recorder, Reporter, Time-keeper, Skeptic (asks 'What is the evidence?') and Materials Monitor.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the phenomenon picture or sketch (goat, fish, dog, lizard) on the board. Say: 'Yesterday we saw that the kidney has millions of nephrons. Today we ask: what exactly happens inside one nephron to turn blood into urine?' Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before calling on anyone. Cold-call 4 pairs with: 'What do you predict leaves the blood and what stays?' Record all predictions on the board without judging; circle disagreements, for example whether glucose is found in urine. Say: 'Some of you think glucose is lost in urine. Keep that as a claim we will test with evidence.' Assign roles quickly so each learner has a duty, and rotate who handles the device.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share surfaces prior ideas and misconceptions (for example, that urine is simply filtered blood, or that the kidney removes only waste). Individual thinking time ensures every learner commits to a prediction, creating a reason to watch the animation closely. This is the Predict step of Predict-Observe-Explain, so the later evidence is compared to their own ideas.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) at least 80% of learners have written a prediction before pairing; (2) number of pairs that mention both 'filtering' and 'taking back' of useful substances; (3) misconceptions recorded on the board (e.g., 'glucose leaves in urine', 'all water leaves'). Oral probe: 'Why would the body not want to lose all the glucose from the ugali you ate?' Tally predictions to compare with post-animation understanding.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups watch the nephron animation clips on one shared device (a phone, tablet or laptop; clips are pre-loaded offline). Clip 1: blood flow into the glomerulus and ultrafiltration into Bowman's capsule under high pressure. Clip 2: selective reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule (glucose, amino acids, salts, water), the loop of Henle, secretion in the distal tubule, and ADH-controlled water reabsorption in the collecting duct. The group watches the first time without writing, the second time pausing at each region, and the third time to check details. Using the 'Follow the Fluid' table, they record for each region (renal artery blood, glomerular filtrate, after proximal tubule, after loop of Henle, urine) what is present or changed for glucose, proteins, urea, water and salts, using arrows or approximate amounts (high, medium, low, none). Each learner also annotates a blank nephron diagram with labels: glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct, and writes what happens at each site. Groups without direct viewing access (back of the group) rotate seats at the half-way point so everyone sees the screen closely.
framework.teacherMoves: Before starting, say: 'Your job is to follow one drop of fluid, like a matatu following its route, and write down what is added or removed at each stop.' Model pausing the clip at the glomerulus and ask: 'Why are blood cells and large proteins not in the filtrate?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups. Circulate every 3-4 minutes: check that the Device Manager is pausing clips at the right points, the Recorder fills the table, and everyone contributes. Ask probing questions: 'What does the animation show happening to glucose in the proximal tubule? Where is the evidence?' 'Why is the urine more concentrated at the end?' Intervene where groups confuse filtration with reabsorption by asking: 'Which one is pressure-driven, and which one needs carrier proteins and energy?' For large classes, stagger sets of questions so two or three groups at a time get your attention, and use group Reporters to share. If a device fails, merge groups or project one clip for the class and keep the table activity going.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain: students compare observed animation evidence with their predictions. Tracing the fluid composition as a table and annotated diagram is a structured data-tracking approach that helps learners see patterns: what is filtered by size, what is reabsorbed by need, and what is concentrated. Using the 'follow the drop' analogy builds mental models of cause and effect along the nephron.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check annotated nephron diagrams and the 'Follow the Fluid' table against indicators: (1) glomerulus labelled with ultrafiltration of small molecules (water, glucose, urea, salts) and exclusion of blood cells and proteins; (2) glucose shown as 100% reabsorbed by the end of the proximal tubule; (3) urea shown as concentrated in urine; (4) water reabsorption linked to the loop of Henle and collecting duct. Oral probes at each group: 'Which part of the nephron does filtering?' Mark each group on a quick checklist (secure / partially / not yet). Look for the Recorder and Skeptic actively using evidence language such as 'The animation shows...'.

framework.learnerExperience: Using their table and annotated diagrams, groups build a concept map or flowchart: Blood in renal artery → glomerulus (ultrafiltration) → Bowman's capsule → proximal tubule (reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, most water and salts) → loop of Henle (concentrating the medulla) → distal tubule (secretion, adjusting salts and pH) → collecting duct (ADH-controlled water reabsorption) → ureter → bladder → urine. They then write a claim-evidence-reasoning explanation for the phenomenon: 'The goat produces concentrated urine because ___ (evidence from nephron). A freshwater fish produces dilute urine because ___.' They link ADH to the dog panting on a hot afternoon: when the body loses water, more ADH is released, so the collecting duct reabsorbs more water. They also discuss what would happen if the proximal tubule failed to reabsorb glucose, linking to diabetes mellitus (glucose in urine) as a Kenyan health example. Groups then present a one-minute explanation to another group.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Turn your table into a story: what is the journey of a glucose molecule and what is the journey of a urea molecule?' Give 8 minutes for the flowchart. Pose: 'The goat drinks water yet produces concentrated urine. Use your nephron evidence to explain.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 different learners to explain one step each, building a chain. Challenge with: 'What would urine look like if the glomerulus was damaged and let proteins through?' Introduce ADH briefly: 'When the goat has lost water through sweating or has not drunk, the brain releases ADH. What does ADH do in the collecting duct?' Prompt connecting to freshwater fish: 'Fish take in water by osmosis. What would their kidneys need to do differently?' Correct misconceptions: urine is not simply filtered blood; reabsorption returns useful substances. Use peer review: groups swap flowcharts and add one 'star' (a correct feature) and one 'wish' (something missing). Validate correct language such as ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concept Mapping/Flowcharts convert the animation into a structured causal chain, making relationships between structure and function explicit. Claim-Evidence-Reasoning links evidence in the table to the phenomenon, and peer review forces learners to justify their reasoning. Connecting ADH to a negative feedback loop prepares the ground for the homeostatic feedback loops in later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect flowcharts and assess against indicators: (1) correct ordering of at least six stages; (2) ultrafiltration described as pressure-driven and size-dependent; (3) selective reabsorption described as returning glucose, amino acids, and water; (4) concentrated urine explained by water reabsorption controlled by ADH. Concept check quiz (5 questions, 4 minutes): (1) Name the site of ultrafiltration. (2) Why is glucose absent from urine in a healthy person? (3) Which hormone controls water reabsorption? (4) Name one substance secreted into the tubule. (5) Why does a goat's urine become more concentrated on a hot day? Score by show of fingers or quick tally; follow up where fewer than 70% are correct.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups return to the class Driving Question Board. They (1) place a sticky note with one answered question from earlier lessons, for example 'How does the kidney make urine?' with a short answer, and (2) write one new question that the nephron evidence raises, for example 'What happens when the kidney fails?', 'Can the dog pant to remove urea?', 'Do fish nephrons have a loop of Henle?', or 'What other organs help remove waste?'. They sort questions into categories: kidney function, other organs, environmental responses, and disease. Each group reads out one new question.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our board. Which questions can we now answer using nephron evidence? Move those to the Answered column and write the evidence.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups to share. Gently guide towards the next lesson: 'We have focused on the kidney. But the dog is also panting and the lizard is basking. Is the kidney the only organ removing wastes?' Highlight any student question about sweating, breathing out carbon dioxide or the liver, and say: 'This question will drive our next investigation.' Ensure each group posts at least one question and that quieter learners get to read theirs out. Redirect off-topic questions politely by parking them on a 'Later' section.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board discussions make learning visible and student-owned. Moving questions to 'Answered' with evidence shows progress, while new questions generate purpose for the next lesson. Sorting questions helps learners see connections between the kidney, other organs and animal adaptations.
framework.formativeAssessment: Count the number of new questions per group and classify them as factual or deep (explaining why/how). Indicators of progress: at least 3 questions about other excretory organs; questions that link structure to function; learners using terms such as 'reabsorption' and 'filtrate' correctly. Oral probe: 'How does your new question relate to the goat and the fish?'. Exit ticket (below) is given at the end of this phase or the next.

framework.learnerExperience: Individually and then in groups, learners revise the class model of how animals keep a balanced internal environment and remove wastes. Starting from their previous model (kidney structure and excretory structures of different animals), they add a labelled nephron diagram and arrows showing inputs (blood with glucose, urea, water, salts), processes (ultrafiltration, reabsorption, secretion, ADH control) and outputs (urine and reabsorbed substances returning to blood). They add a short label connecting the model to the goat (concentrated urine when water is scarce) and the freshwater fish (large volumes of dilute urine when water floods in). They mark a '?' on the model where they do not yet know how the body gets rid of other wastes (sweat, bile, carbon dioxide). Learners complete an exit ticket: (1) One thing I figured out about urine formation: ___ (2) One thing I am still wondering: ___ (3) Complete: Glucose is not in urine because ___.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your model from the last lesson. What new parts must you add from the nephron evidence? What must you change?' Give 8 minutes for revision. Circulate and look for models that show a process rather than just labels. Pause and ask: 'Where on your model is the pressure that pushes fluid out of the blood? Where is the energy-using step?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then cold-call 3 learners to explain revisions. Use peer review: groups swap and give one comment, 'One thing I like is ___; one thing to add is ___.' Point to the '?' marks and say: 'Our model explains how the kidney removes urea and balances water. But the dog is panting and the goat is sweating. Which other organs might help? We will investigate this in the next lesson.' Collect exit tickets at the door and use them to plan reteaching.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model Building & Revision requires learners to integrate new evidence into a cumulative explanation of the phenomenon, making their thinking visible and revisable. Marking gaps with '?' builds a need for further evidence. Peer review strengthens scientific argumentation and communication.
framework.formativeAssessment: Assess the revised model using indicators: (1) nephron stages in the correct sequence with labels; (2) arrows show reabsorption returning to blood; (3) clear link between ADH and urine concentration; (4) goat and fish contrasted in the model; (5) at least one '?' identifying an unanswered question. Exit ticket sorting: green (can explain ultrafiltration and reabsorption), yellow (can name stages but not explain), red (confuses stages). Plan a 5-minute reteach at the start of the next lesson for red group learners.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Did every learner in the large groups get a chance to see the screen and contribute, or did one or two dominate the device? Which part of the nephron was hardest to understand (probably selective reabsorption versus secretion or the loop of Henle)? Did learners link the nephron process back to the goat and the fish without prompting? Which misconceptions persisted (for example, that urine is just filtered blood or that glucose is lost in urine)? Review exit tickets to decide who needs reteaching, and consider whether the animation pace or group size should change. Think about how to connect the next lesson on other excretory organs (liver, skin, lungs) to the questions learners posted on the DQB, and whether role rotation improved participation.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We watched animations of the nephron and traced how blood, filtrate and urine differ in glucose, protein, urea and water. We saw that blood cells and proteins stay in the blood, glucose is fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, and urine is concentrated by water reabsorption in the loop of Henle and collecting duct.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Urine formation involves ultrafiltration in the glomerulus (small molecules forced into Bowman's capsule under high pressure), followed by selective reabsorption of useful substances and secretion of extra wastes and ions in the nephron tubule. ADH controls how much water is reabsorbed, so urine can be concentrated or dilute.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: A goat that loses water on a hot day releases more ADH, so its collecting ducts reabsorb more water and it produces small amounts of concentrated urine. A freshwater fish gains water by osmosis, so it produces large amounts of dilute urine. New question: What other organs in mammals assist in excretion besides the kidney?

LESSONS.title: Liver and Skin: Hidden Waste Processors Behind the Hot Afternoon
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.3: Excretion and Homeostasis in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: liver, hepatocyte, deamination, urea, bile, bilirubin, skin, epidermis, dermis, sweat gland, sweat secretion, cirrhosis, hepatitis, fatty liver disease, excretion, homeostasis

slo.purpose: Learners relate the structure of the mammalian liver and skin to their excretory and detoxifying functions, and use this evidence to explain how a panting dog, a goat and other animals remove metabolic wastes and keep the body stable on a hot afternoon.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (d) relate the structure of the mammalian liver and skin to their excretory functions. The learner identifies hepatocytes, sinusoids, bile canaliculi, the epidermis, dermis, sweat glands and blood capillaries on photomicrographs and illustrations. The learner describes deamination (amino acids to urea), bile pigment production (breakdown of haemoglobin to bilirubin) and sweat secretion (water, salts and a little urea), and outlines the effects of cirrhosis, hepatitis and fatty liver disease.
slo.skills: Observing and interpreting photomicrographs (NGSS SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data); drawing and annotating structures (SEP: Developing and Using Models); constructing explanations from evidence (SEP: Constructing Explanations); asking questions of a resource person (SEP: Asking Questions); Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: asking questions to be clear on what they need.
slo.attitudes: Responsibility: engaging in assigned group roles and duties. Social Justice: sharing the limited charts, slides and devices equitably. Waste Management and Environmental Conservation: appreciating how organisms manage their wastes and how healthy living protects the liver.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do animals get rid of waste products? 2. How do animals cope with environmental changes?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 to 3 gathered evidence on excretory products and organs in insects, birds and fish and on the kidney and nephron. Lesson 4 adds two organs not yet considered: the liver, which makes the urea the kidney removes, and the skin, which excretes sweat and cools the body. It closes a gap in the model: the kidney is not the only organ of excretion and homeostasis. It also leads to Lesson 5: How does the body keep internal water, temperature and sugar levels constant during external changes?
slo.safetyNotes: Handle glass slides and microscopes carefully and report breakages immediately. Do not touch broken glass. Wash hands after handling any materials. If fresh kidneys from earlier lessons are still in the room, keep them covered in trays and wear gloves. Be sensitive to learners with family members who have liver disease or alcohol-related illness; keep discussion factual and respectful. The resource person must not give personal medical advice. Remind learners to avoid self-medication and to seek clinic advice.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the hot-afternoon phenomenon (panting dog, still lizard, goats, freshwater fish) and ask: where does the urea in a goat's urine come from, and what does sweat do for a dog-like mammal such as a human in Kisumu at noon? They predict the roles of the liver and skin, examine photomicrographs, charts and illustrations of liver and skin histology in groups, discuss deamination, bile production and sweat secretion, and hear a resource person (a clinical officer, nurse or laboratory technologist) explain cirrhosis, hepatitis and fatty liver disease. They build explanations linking structure to function, update the Driving Question Board with the new question about keeping water, temperature and sugar constant, and revise the class model so that the liver and skin sit alongside the kidney.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners look at the phenomenon image again (dog panting, lizard on rock, goats, freshwater fish). Individually, in their notebooks, they answer: (1) Goat urine contains urea. Where in the body is urea made? (2) Humans at a Mombasa beach sweat heavily. What is in sweat and why is it released? (3) What do you think the liver does besides storing food? They draw a quick sketch of where they think the liver and skin fit into the body's waste removal and write one confident idea and one uncertainty. Then Think-Pair-Share: they compare predictions with a partner and note one agreement and one disagreement.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the phenomenon image. Say: 'Last lesson we followed urea through the nephron. Today we ask: where did that urea come from, and what else is leaving the body on a hot afternoon?' Give 3 minutes of silent writing. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after each question before taking any response. Say: 'I am not looking for the right answer yet; I want your best thinking.' Circulate and note common ideas (for example 'the liver only stores food', 'sweat is only water', 'urea is made in the kidney'). Cold-call 4 pairs: 'Pair 3, what did you agree on? Pair 7, what did you disagree on?' Record the predictions on the board under the heading 'Our first ideas' without correcting them. Ask one probing question: 'What would make you change your mind?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share inside a Predict-Observe-Explain cycle. Making predictions in writing first surfaces preconceptions (for example that urea is made in the kidney), creates a need to know and gives learners a personal stake in the evidence they will see. Pairing lets learners rehearse ideas safely before sharing in a large class.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: at least 4 of 5 sampled notebooks show a prediction for each of the 3 questions; learners can state where they think urea is made; the teacher tallies on the board how many pairs think the kidney makes urea versus the liver. Oral probe: 'Why do you think that?' requires a reason, not only an answer. Misconceptions recorded for comparison in the Explain Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) In groups of 5-6 (roles: materials manager, recorder, drawer, reporter, timekeeper) learners rotate through three stations with shared resources. Station A, Liver histology: examine a photomicrograph/chart of liver tissue (and a microscope slide where available). Identify hepatocytes, sinusoids, central vein, hepatic portal vein and bile canaliculi. Draw and annotate a labelled sketch and answer: how does blood flow past the hepatocytes? Station B, Skin histology: examine a skin section chart/photomicrograph. Identify epidermis, dermis, sweat gland, sweat duct, pore, blood capillaries, hair follicle and erector muscle. Annotate where sweat is made and released and how blood vessels near the surface help cooling. Station C, Function cards: read short cards on deamination (excess amino acids lose the amino group which forms ammonia, then urea, carried by blood to the kidneys), bile (bilirubin from old red blood cells is excreted in bile, which also emulsifies fats) and sweat (water, salts and a little urea lost from the skin; evaporation cools the body). Complete a table: Structure, Substance removed or processed, Where it goes. Learners apply it to the phenomenon: a goat on a hot afternoon digesting dry grass, and a human walking in Nairobi in the heat. Every group takes about 8 minutes per station.
framework.teacherMoves: Set up stations before class using the available charts, photomicrographs and slides. Where there are not enough slides or charts, laminate or copy pages from the textbook so every group has something. Say: 'You are scientists reading tissue, not just labelling a picture. For each structure, ask: what is it, and what job does its shape suggest?' Assign roles and say: 'Materials managers, you are responsible for fair sharing; nobody keeps the chart for more than 8 minutes.' Ring a bell for rotation. Circulate with oral probes: 'Why are the sinusoids so wide and thin-walled? What does that allow between blood and hepatocytes?' and 'Why is the sweat gland coiled and surrounded by capillaries?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after each probe before prompting. Cold-call 3 groups for each station at the end: 'Group 2, tell us one structure and the job its shape suggests.' Remind learners to wash hands if they handled any biological material and to carry microscopes with both hands.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (observation step) combined with Analyzing and Interpreting Data. Rotating stations let a large class gather the same evidence with limited resources. The 'shape suggests job' prompt trains learners to reason from structure to function, the core idea of this sub-strand, and the function cards link the images to the chemistry of wastes so learners connect the liver and skin to the phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: annotated sketches show at least 4 correctly labelled structures for the liver and 5 for the skin; the completed table has a correct entry for deamination (urea to the kidney), bile (bilirubin to the intestine) and sweat (water, salts, urea via the skin); learners can say why sinusoids and sweat gland capillaries are important. Oral probes: 'What would happen to urea in the blood if the liver could not deaminate amino acids?' Teacher checks and initials annotated diagrams during rotation.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Part 1 (10 min): Learners return to their predictions and revise them in a different colour, using evidence from the stations. They then build a short Concept Map/flowchart: Protein in a meal of beans or ugali with sukuma wiki, amino acids, liver (deamination), ammonia, urea, blood, kidney, urine. They add a second branch: old red blood cells, liver, bilirubin, bile, intestine, faeces, and a third branch: heat, sweat glands, sweat, evaporation, cooling. Part 2 (15 min): A resource person (clinical officer, nurse or laboratory technologist from the local health centre) gives a 10-minute talk on cirrhosis, hepatitis and fatty liver disease: causes (viruses, excess alcohol, fatty diet, obesity), symptoms (jaundice, swelling, tiredness) and prevention (hepatitis B vaccination, hygiene, balanced diet, avoiding alcohol). Learners prepare questions, then relate one disorder to a structural loss: for example, scarring in cirrhosis damages hepatocytes and reduces blood flow so urea and bilirubin build up and jaundice results. They finish with a Think-Pair-Share: 'Which of our animals on the hot afternoon rely most on the skin to lose heat, and which rely little on it? Why?' (for example, humans and horses sweat, dogs pant because they have few sweat glands, lizards do not sweat).
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Pick up your coloured pen. Cross nothing out; show me how your thinking changed.' Draw the first branch of the concept map on the board and invite learners to complete the rest in their groups. Move between groups and ask: 'What links this arrow? What is the evidence?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before calling on anyone. Cold-call 5 learners to add one box or arrow each to a class map, asking each: 'What evidence from the stations supports that?' Introduce the resource person and set norms: 'We listen respectfully and ask scientific questions, not personal medical ones.' Before the talk, say: 'Write down one question you would like answered.' After the talk, ask 3 learners to give questions and discuss them. Pose: 'If cirrhosis scars the liver, which structure from our photomicrograph is affected and what happens to the waste in the blood?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds, then collect answers from 4 pairs. Correct misconceptions explicitly, for example: 'Urea is made in the liver and removed by the kidney.' Link back: 'So the goat's urea began in its liver. The kidney only cleared it.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concept Mapping/Flowcharts plus Think-Pair-Share. A flowchart forces learners to connect organs, substances and direction of movement, so liver, blood, kidney and skin become one system rather than separate facts. Applying the map to disorders makes learners reason from damaged structure to disrupted function, and to the animals in the phenomenon (panting dog, still lizard) to compare different strategies for heat loss.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: revised predictions show a correct statement that urea is made in the liver; concept maps include deamination, urea, bile and sweat with correctly directed arrows; at least 3 learners can explain why liver damage leads to jaundice. Concept check quiz (5 minutes, 4 questions): (1) Name the process that forms urea. (2) What pigment is excreted in bile? (3) Name two substances in sweat. (4) State one cause of fatty liver disease. Teacher scans for 70 percent correct and notes who needs re-teaching.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners add to the class Driving Question Board. Each group writes 1-2 new questions on sticky notes arising from today (for example: 'If sweat cools us, why do dogs pant instead?' 'Why do we feel thirsty after sweating?' 'How does the body know when to sweat?'). They also place sticky notes under 'Questions we can now answer' (for example, 'Where is urea made?') and 'Questions we still have'. The class sorts the questions into themes (water, temperature, sugar levels). Learners notice that many questions ask how the body keeps conditions constant when the outside changes, which leads to the next lesson.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look back at our big question: how do different animals maintain a balanced internal environment? What did the liver and skin add?' Give each group 2 minutes to write questions. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after asking: 'What do you notice about these questions?' Cold-call 4 groups to read and place a note and explain the link to the phenomenon. Move answered questions to the 'Can answer' column with learners naming the evidence. Highlight three clusters and say: 'These questions are about keeping water, temperature and sugar steady. That is exactly what we investigate next lesson: how does the body keep internal water, temperature and sugar levels constant during external changes?' Photograph the DQB for records.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (DQB) discussion. The DQB makes learners' questions visible, shows how evidence answers some of them while raising others, and gives learners ownership of the learning path. Sorting into themes turns scattered curiosity into a shared purpose for the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: each group contributes at least one new, testable question; at least 2 notes are moved to 'Can answer' with a named piece of evidence; learners link a question to the phenomenon, for example 'dog pants because...'. Teacher records the question themes and which groups still ask only recall questions (what, where) instead of mechanism questions (how, why).

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners revise the class model (a large poster of the whole body with the kidney, ureter, bladder, gills of fish, and Malpighian tubules from earlier lessons) by adding the liver and skin. In groups they add labelled arrows for: amino acids to liver to urea to blood to kidney; haemoglobin breakdown to bile to intestine; heat to sweat glands to evaporation. Then they write an individual exit ticket explaining: 'Using the liver or skin, explain how a goat or a human removes wastes or loses heat on a hot afternoon in Kisumu, and what is still missing from our model?' Groups peer review each other's additions using 'two stars and a wish'.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model must now explain more of the phenomenon. Add the liver and skin, and show the direction of every arrow.' Provide markers and sticky notes so each group has a share of the poster. Circulate and ask: 'Where does the urea come from before the kidney gets it? What carries it?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds.
