Cold-call 3 groups to explain one new addition to the class. Hand out exit tickets and say: 'Write in full sentences with at least two pieces of evidence.' Collect exit tickets at the door. Close with: 'We now know that more than one organ removes wastes, but we do not yet know how the body keeps water, temperature and sugar steady while the outside changes. That is our next question.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model Building and Revision. Updating a shared model makes learners integrate new evidence with earlier evidence from the kidney, fish gills and insects, and shows what the model can and cannot yet explain (for example, why the dog pants and the lizard basks). Peer review builds scientific argumentation and shared responsibility.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: model includes the liver and skin with correct arrow directions and labels; exit tickets name deamination or sweating and give a correct function; at least 80 percent of exit tickets state one remaining gap (for example, the control of temperature or sugar). Peer review uses 'two stars and a wish' written on sticky notes. Teacher sorts exit tickets into 'secure', 'partly secure' and 'not yet' to plan a 5-minute reteach at the start of Lesson 5.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: 1. Which structure-function link did learners find hardest (sinusoids, deamination or sweat glands), and what evidence in the annotated sketches and quiz showed this? 2. Did the stations give every learner a fair chance to see the images despite limited charts and slides? What would you change for large classes? 3. How well did the resource person link disease to the structure learners had just observed, and did learners ask scientific rather than personal questions? 4. Did learners still believe the kidney makes urea after the lesson? How do you know? 5. Which DQB questions show readiness for Lesson 5 on water, temperature and sugar regulation, and which learners need more support? 6. Were any learners uncomfortable discussing liver disease, and how did you handle it?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed photomicrographs and charts of the liver (hepatocytes, sinusoids, bile canaliculi) and skin (epidermis, dermis, sweat glands, capillaries), and heard about cirrhosis, hepatitis and fatty liver disease.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The liver deaminates excess amino acids to make urea, breaks down haemoglobin to make bile pigments and processes toxic substances; the skin excretes sweat containing water, salts and a little urea and helps cool the body. Liver disorders damage these functions.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Urea in the goat's urine begins in the liver, is carried by blood to the kidney and removed, while sweat or panting helps animals lose heat on a hot afternoon. The liver and skin work with the kidney to remove wastes and keep the body stable, but we still need to explain how water, temperature and sugar levels are kept constant.

LESSONS.title: Feedback Loops: How the Body Keeps Water and Blood Glucose Steady
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.3: Excretion and Homeostasis in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: homeostasis, negative feedback, osmoregulation, ADH, insulin, glucagon, diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus, set point, receptor, effector

slo.purpose: Learners use feedback flowcharts and case studies to explain how negative feedback regulates water balance (ADH) and blood glucose (insulin and glucagon) in humans, and how this helps explain why goats and freshwater fish handle water so differently on a hot afternoon.
slo.knowledge: e) illustrate homeostatic regulation in humans. Learners explain that negative feedback detects a change from a set point and triggers a response that reverses it. They describe osmoregulation (osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus, ADH from the posterior pituitary, kidney collecting ducts) and blood sugar regulation (pancreatic islet cells, insulin, glucagon, liver). They distinguish diabetes mellitus from diabetes insipidus.
slo.skills: Constructing and interpreting flowcharts and concept maps (NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models); analysing case study data (SEP: Analyzing and Interpreting Data); constructing evidence-based explanations (SEP: Constructing Explanations); asking clarifying questions (Critical Thinking and Problem Solving); collaboration in shared-resource groups.
slo.attitudes: Social Justice: shares resources equitably (charts, case study sheets, devices) within the group. Responsibility: takes on assigned roles and completes them. Appreciation of homeostasis as vital to health and of the need to conserve biodiversity (PCI: Environmental Conservation). Empathy for people living with diabetes.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do animals get rid of waste products? 2. How do animals cope with environmental changes?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-4 established excretory products and organs and how the kidney forms urine. Lesson 5 shows that the kidney's output is not fixed but controlled by negative feedback. This explains why the goat (conserving water) produces concentrated urine while the freshwater fish produces dilute urine, and why the body's internal conditions stay steady. It also raises a new question for Lesson 6: how is core temperature kept stable when the weather changes, as in the panting dog and the basking lizard?
slo.safetyNotes: Hand-washing after handling any specimens. For the glucose demonstration or sugary drinks, no tasting of lab materials. Handle case studies on diabetes sensitively; do not ask learners to disclose personal or family health conditions. If kidney specimens from earlier lessons are still on display, keep them covered, use gloves, and dispose of them as directed by the teacher. Ensure no learner is pressured to take part in any fasting or sugar activity.

LESSONS.overview: Return to the anchoring phenomenon: the goat drinks water yet makes concentrated urine, while the freshwater fish continually excretes dilute urine. Learners first predict what the body does when it loses too much water on a hot day in Kisumu or Nairobi, and what happens to blood sugar after a meal of ugali and sukuma wiki. In groups of 5-6 (one set of charts and one device per group), they build feedback flowcharts for ADH osmoregulation and insulin/glucagon blood sugar control using homeostasis feedback charts. They then evaluate case studies of diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus to test their flowcharts by locating where each loop breaks. Using Predict-Observe-Explain, they apply the idea of nephron function from the kidney dissection to explain how ADH changes urine concentration. The class updates the Driving Question Board and revises its cumulative model by adding negative feedback control. The lesson ends with the question of how body temperature is regulated.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at a short scenario on the board: Wanjiku runs 10 km in the hot afternoon at Kericho, sweats a lot and drinks little water. Later she eats a big plate of ugali and beans and a mandazi with sweet tea. In pairs (Think-Pair-Share) they individually sketch or write predictions for (a) what happens to her urine volume and concentration, and (b) what happens to her blood sugar after the meal and how the body brings it back to normal. They link back to the goat and the freshwater fish by predicting which animal's kidney is more like Wanjiku's after the run.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the scenario and the phenomenon picture (goat and fish). Say: "Take 2 minutes to think silently. Write what you think happens to her urine, and what happens to her blood sugar. Use arrows if it helps." WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each question before taking answers. Then: "Turn to your partner and share for 2 minutes. Look for where you disagree." Cold-call 4 pairs: "Pair 3, what did you predict happens to the urine? What made you think that?" Record predictions on the board in two columns (water, glucose) without correcting them. Ask: "Who predicted the body does something to reverse the change? What would that be?" Circulate and note common ideas such as 'the kidney just filters more'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share surfaces prior ideas about the kidney and sugar and creates a record of initial thinking. Predicting before the evidence gives learners a stake in the investigation and lets them compare later ideas to their predictions, linking to Lessons 3-4 on urine formation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: learners write a prediction with a reason, not just a statement; at least 3 of 4 cold-called pairs can state a cause-effect link (e.g., 'less water, so less urine'). Note on a checklist who mentions a control or reversing mechanism, and who holds misconceptions such as 'sugar is just removed in urine in everyone' or 'the kidney decides on its own'. Oral probes: "What is your evidence for that?"

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 5-6 with assigned roles (reader, flowchart builder, recorder, materials manager, reporter), learners use the homeostasis feedback charts to gather evidence. Part A: from the chart, they assemble an osmoregulation flowchart on manila paper using cards: dehydration (blood too concentrated) → osmoreceptors in hypothalamus → posterior pituitary releases more ADH → collecting duct becomes more permeable → more water reabsorbed → small volume of concentrated urine → blood water returns to normal → ADH falls. They then draw the opposite loop for drinking lots of water. Part B: they build a blood glucose flowchart: high glucose after a meal → beta cells of islets of Langerhans release insulin → liver and muscle take up glucose and convert it to glycogen, cells use more → glucose falls; low glucose (after a long run or fasting) → alpha cells release glucagon → liver converts glycogen to glucose → glucose rises. Part C: they read two case studies. Case 1, diabetes mellitus (a 15-year-old in Nakuru with excessive thirst, frequent urination, glucose in urine, high blood glucose; Type 1 shows too little insulin). Case 2, diabetes insipidus (a patient in Kisumu passing up to 10 litres of very dilute urine daily, always thirsty, normal blood glucose, low ADH or kidney not responding to ADH). They mark on their flowcharts where the loop is broken in each case. Where possible, a group views the short feedback animation on the shared device (one device per group, rotating viewer roles).
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute materials: "Materials managers, collect one chart set, one case study sheet and the card set for your group. Share equally; every member must handle the cards." Model with the first card: "A negative feedback loop has a set point, a receptor, a control centre, an effector and a response. Find these in the chart." Circulate with a checklist, asking oral probes: "Which structure detects the change? Which one responds? Why do we call this negative feedback?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds after each probe. Cold-call 3 groups to explain one arrow: "Group 2, why does more ADH mean less urine?" Prompt for a link to Lesson 4: "Which part of the nephron does ADH act on?" For case studies: "Underline the symptoms. Which step in your flowchart could fail to give these symptoms?" Extend with a question: "Why do diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus both cause thirst and a lot of urine, but only one has sugar in the urine?" Manage the large class by giving a 5-minute time check for each part, using group roles, and having groups with devices share with a neighbouring group if needed. Safety: remind about caring and respectful discussion of illness.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concept Mapping/Flowcharts: constructing the loops as cause-effect chains forces learners to identify receptors, control centres and effectors and to see why the change is reversed. Case studies act as a test of the model: learners use the flowchart to locate the failure that produces each set of symptoms. Collaborative role assignment builds equitable participation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: flowchart shows a complete loop with a return arrow to the set point; ADH and insulin/glucagon are correctly placed; the case studies are correctly marked (diabetes mellitus: insulin missing or ineffective; diabetes insipidus: ADH missing or ineffective). Peer review: groups swap flowcharts and give one 'star' and one 'step' using a 3-point checklist (complete loop, correct hormones, correct direction of change). Oral probes recorded for at least 8 learners.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their Predict-phase notes. Using Predict-Observe-Explain, each group writes a short explanation (4-6 sentences plus a labelled nephron sketch) of what happens in Wanjiku's body after the run and the meal, then explains how this reasoning applies to the goat and freshwater fish: the goat conserves water so ADH is high and urine is concentrated, while freshwater fish absorb water by osmosis and excrete dilute urine in large volume. Learners annotate their nephron diagrams from the kidney dissection to show where ADH acts (collecting duct) and where glucose is normally fully reabsorbed (proximal convoluted tubule), explaining why glucose appears in the urine in diabetes mellitus. Then a concept check quiz (5 questions) is completed individually.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look back at your prediction. What did you get right, and what do you want to change? Use evidence from the flowchart." WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners from different groups: "What would happen to Wanjiku's ADH level, and why?" and "What would happen to her blood sugar after the mandazi, and which hormone acts?" Press for reasoning with: "How do you know? Which part of the chart shows that?" Address misconceptions: ADH is not a waste product; insulin does not remove sugar from the body, it moves it into cells and stores it as glycogen; diabetes insipidus is unrelated to sugar. Challenge: "Fish and goats both have kidneys. What does the idea of feedback tell us about why their urine differs?" Note that the fish also uses regulation of salt and water but not necessarily through the same hormone pathway, so learners should explain in terms of the direction of water movement. Administer the quiz: "Put pens down at the sound of the signal; no talking during the quiz." Collect for quick marking.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain closes the loop by having learners compare their predictions to the evidence and revise their reasoning. Writing a causal explanation with a diagram helps them connect the macro phenomenon (urine concentration, thirst) to the micro mechanism (hormones acting on the nephron).
framework.formativeAssessment: Concept check quiz (5 items): 1) Define negative feedback. 2) Name the hormone released when blood is too concentrated. 3) State the effect of insulin on blood glucose. 4) Name the organ that converts glycogen to glucose under glucagon. 5) Give one difference between diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus. Success criterion: 4/5 correct. Annotated nephron diagram check: ADH correctly placed at the collecting duct, a correct arrow showing water reabsorption. Record learners below 3/5 for reteaching in the next lesson.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the Driving Question Board with the question: 'How do different animals maintain a balanced internal environment and eliminate toxic wastes despite drastic changes in their external conditions?' Each group writes on sticky notes (a) one question that has now been answered (with evidence from today) and (b) one new question. They place answered questions in an 'Answered' column with a short evidence note, and new questions in a 'Still to investigate' column. Likely new questions: 'How does the dog's panting help keep it cool?' 'Why does the lizard bask?' 'Do fish use ADH?' They also complete an exit ticket.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Look at the board. Which of our questions can we now answer? Bring your sticky note and explain the evidence." WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 groups to place and justify notes: "What evidence from today supports your answer?" Guide the gap: "We have explained water and blood sugar. But look at the dog and the lizard. What have we not yet explained?" Draw out the temperature question and write it on the board as the lead-in: "How does the body keep core temperature stable when the outside weather changes drastically?" Hand out exit ticket slips and set 3 minutes: "Write one thing you understand, one thing you are unsure about, and draw the loop for one hormone."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: The DQB makes progress visible and keeps the class focused on a shared, student-generated question. Sorting questions into answered and new builds a sense of purpose and shows how today's evidence connects to the next investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket: learners complete a mini-loop for either ADH or insulin/glucagon and state one question remaining. Success indicators: the loop includes stimulus, receptor, hormone, effector and response; questions refer to temperature or other animals. Quick sort of tickets into three piles: secure, partly secure, not yet secure, to plan the start of Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups revisit the class model of how animals maintain a balanced internal environment (started in earlier lessons and including excretory organs, kidney structure and urine formation). They add a layer for control: negative feedback loops with ADH and insulin/glucagon, placing arrows from the brain or pancreas to the kidney or liver. They add a link to the goat and the freshwater fish, showing high versus low ADH-type water conservation, and note what the model cannot yet explain (temperature, behavioural responses such as basking and panting). Groups do a gallery walk and peer review the physical or drawn models of two other groups, using sticky notes with one strength and one suggestion.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Take out your model from last lesson. What needs to be added or changed to show how the body keeps water and sugar steady?" WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Ask groups to revise for 8 minutes. Prompt: "Where is the set point? What is the feedback arrow? What happens if that part fails?" During the gallery walk say: "Visit two other groups. Give one strength and one suggestion; use evidence, not opinion." Cold-call 3 groups to share a change they made and why: "What did you change, and what evidence made you change it?" Close by linking to the next lesson: "Our model explains water and sugar. It cannot yet explain why the dog pants or the lizard basks. In Lesson 6 we will investigate temperature regulation." Ask learners to store models safely for later revision.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model Building & Revision: adding feedback loops shows that homeostasis is a dynamic process, not a static state. Peer review of models makes learners justify their representations with evidence and identify gaps that motivate the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators for the model: includes labelled negative feedback loops with a return to the set point; correctly links ADH to the kidney and insulin/glucagon to the liver and pancreas; connects at least one loop to the goat or the fish; records one limitation. Peer review sticky notes use evidence-based comments. Oral probe: "What would happen to the model if ADH were missing?" Record how many groups can answer with diabetes insipidus symptoms.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners could describe the feedback loop in their own words and which only copied the chart? Did learners confuse diabetes mellitus and insipidus, and which case-study prompts cleared this up? Was the group size right for sharing the charts and the single device? Did the quiz and exit tickets show who needs reteaching on hormones and nephron locations? How well did learners link the loops back to the goat, the fish, and the other animals? Which new questions on the DQB lead naturally into temperature regulation for Lesson 6?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that hormone signals such as ADH, insulin and glucagon form feedback loops, and that in diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus the symptoms (thirst, lots of urine, sugar in urine or very dilute urine) show where a loop has failed.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that negative feedback detects a change from a set point and triggers a response that reverses it; ADH adjusts how much water the kidney reabsorbs, and insulin and glucagon keep blood glucose within a narrow range.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain why the goat can produce concentrated urine to save water while the freshwater fish excretes dilute urine, how the body keeps water and glucose steady after exercise and a meal, and why the next question is how body temperature is kept stable in animals like the dog and the lizard.

LESSONS.title: Keeping Cool and Staying Warm: Thermoregulation in the Dog, the Lizard and Us
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.3: Excretion and Homeostasis in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: thermoregulation, negative feedback, vasodilation, vasoconstriction, sweating, panting, basking, burrowing, hibernation, aestivation, ectotherm, endotherm

slo.purpose: Learners use thermoregulation diagrams, video clips and field observation notes of local animals to figure out how physiological mechanisms (sweating, vasodilation, vasoconstriction) and behavioural adjustments (basking, panting, burrowing, hibernation, aestivation) control body heat, and use feedback loops to explain why the dog pants and the lizard stays still on a warm rock.
slo.knowledge: Learners will explain that thermoregulation is a homeostatic process that keeps body temperature within a narrow range through negative feedback. They will describe how the skin and hypothalamus respond to heat (vasodilation, sweating, panting) and to cold (vasoconstriction, shivering, hair erection). They will distinguish endotherms such as dogs, goats and humans from ectotherms such as lizards, which rely on behaviour (basking, shade-seeking, burrowing). They will also explain hibernation and aestivation as responses to prolonged cold or heat and drought.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (flowcharts of feedback loops); analysing and interpreting data (field observation notes and temperature data); constructing explanations from evidence; asking questions (Critical Thinking and Problem Solving); using digital devices in groups to view video clips (Digital Literacy).
slo.attitudes: Responsibility in carrying out assigned group roles during observation; Social Justice in sharing devices and materials equitably; appreciation of local biodiversity and its conservation (Environmental Conservation PCI); curiosity about how animals in the community survive environmental change.
slo.keyInquiry: How do animals cope with environmental changes? (KICD Key Inquiry Question 2)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 to 5 built evidence on excretory structures and products, the kidney and nephron, urine formation, and the liver and skin. Lesson 6 turns to the other half of the driving question: keeping a steady internal environment as external conditions change. It explains the dog and the lizard in the anchoring phenomenon and shows that temperature control uses the same sensor, control centre, effector and negative-feedback logic as osmoregulation. This raises the question for Lesson 7: Why are excretion and homeostasis so vital for the overall survival of living organisms?
slo.safetyNotes: Conduct field observations from a safe distance. Do not handle lizards, snakes or unfamiliar dogs and goats, and watch out for ticks and sun exposure. Learners wear hats and carry drinking water outdoors. If the class stays indoors, use video clips and observation notes instead. Do not place hot-water or ice demonstrations on bare skin; use lukewarm and cool water only. Wash hands after any outdoor activity. Share devices in groups of 5 to 6 and keep volume low.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the hot afternoon scene: a dog panting, a lizard motionless on a warm rock, goats drinking and fish excreting dilute urine. They first predict why the dog pants and the lizard stays still. In the Observe phase, groups of 5 to 6 share one device or printed set to study thermoregulation diagrams, video clips and field observation notes of local animals (dogs, goats, agama lizards, tortoises, lungfish, frogs, cattle seeking shade at midday in the Rift Valley) responding to weather. They trace feedback loops for heat and cold in a mammal and compare these with the behavioural strategies of an ectotherm. In the Explain phase they build flowcharts and write evidence-based explanations of the dog and the lizard. They then add questions and evidence to the Driving Question Board and revise their cumulative model by adding a temperature-control loop alongside the osmoregulation and excretion components. An exit ticket leads to the question for Lesson 7 on why excretion and homeostasis are vital for survival.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners recall the anchoring scene: the dog panting on a hot afternoon in the community and the lizard sitting motionless on a warm rock. Individually, they write a prediction for 2 minutes answering: 'Why does the dog pant while the lizard stays still on a hot rock? What is each animal doing to its body temperature?' They then do Think-Pair-Share, sketch a quick 'before' arrow diagram of how heat leaves or enters each animal, and record a confidence rating from 1 to 3.
framework.teacherMoves: Display or sketch the scene on the board. Say: 'Picture Kericho at 2 pm. A dog is panting, a lizard is on a hot rock. Write down what each animal is doing to its body temperature, and why.' Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then WAIT TIME of 10 to 15 seconds before pairing. Say: 'Turn to your partner and compare for 1 minute; look for where you disagree.' Cold-call 4 pairs from different parts of the room, including at least 2 who have not spoken this term, and record competing ideas on the board without judging, such as 'dogs sweat like us' or 'lizards are lazy'. Probe: 'What makes you think that? What evidence would change your mind?' Mark unresolved ideas with a star as questions for the Observe phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share (Predict phase of Predict-Observe-Explain): writing a prediction first surfaces learners' prior ideas (for example, that all animals sweat, or that stillness means laziness) so the later evidence can confront them. Pair talk lets every learner rehearse reasoning before the whole class hears it, which supports equitable participation in a large class.
framework.formativeAssessment: Oral probes and prediction sheets. Observable indicators: learners mention heat loss or gain, body temperature, or a link to the environment; learners distinguish panting from sweating; learners give a reason for the lizard's stillness. Note how many predictions use words such as 'cool down', 'warm up' or 'body temperature' versus only describing behaviour. Tally misconceptions on the board to guide the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 5 to 6, with assigned roles (reader, recorder, diagram analyst, device operator, reporter) that rotate between stations, learners work through 3 stations in about 25 minutes. Station 1, Diagrams: they study a thermoregulation diagram of a mammal's skin and hypothalamus on a printed chart, tracing what happens when the blood is too hot or too cold (vasodilation, sweating, panting, vasoconstriction, shivering, hair raising), and annotate the arrows. Station 2, Video clips on the shared device: they watch short clips of a dog panting, an agama lizard basking, shade-seeking and moving into a rock crevice, cattle or goats resting under acacia trees at midday, and, where available, a tortoise or lungfish aestivating or a hibernating animal. They record what the animal does, the environmental condition, and the likely effect on body temperature. Station 3, Field observation notes: they read notes collected by the teacher or learners, for example 'Agama lizard on rock at 9 am, 11 am and 2 pm; moves into shade at 2 pm', 'Dog under mango tree panting at midday', 'Goats rest in shade at noon, graze at 5 pm', and 'Frogs buried in mud during the dry season at Lake Victoria shores'. They tabulate time of day, behaviour, temperature trend and the type of mechanism (physiological or behavioural). Learners who cannot access the device view the clips with another group in turns so that everyone gets a fair turn.
framework.teacherMoves: Before starting, say: 'Your job is to collect evidence of how the body temperature of these animals is controlled. Record what you SEE, not what you assume.' State the safety rules and the roles, and set a timer for 8 minutes per station. Circulate and ask each group at least one probing question: 'What is the blood vessel in the skin doing here, and what does that do to heat loss?' 'Why might the lizard move into shade at 2 pm?' 'How is the dog's panting different from the lizard's behaviour?' After each question WAIT 10 to 15 seconds. If a group says 'the lizard is lazy', respond: 'What does the evidence in your notes show about when it moves?' Where devices are limited, rotate one device across groups and give the others the printed notes first. Pause for 2 minutes at the end and ask 3 cold-called learners to name one observation that surprised them.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence gathering through multiple representations (diagram, video, field notes): comparing the diagram of a mammal's feedback system with real behaviours of local ectotherms and endotherms helps learners see that organisms keep internal conditions steady by different means. Structured recording tables separate observation from inference, and rotating roles ensure shared responsibility.
framework.formativeAssessment: Annotated thermoregulation diagrams and observation tables. Observable indicators: the arrows correctly show vasodilation bringing blood close to the skin surface to lose heat and vasoconstriction reducing blood flow to the skin to conserve heat; the table lists at least 4 animal behaviours with matched environmental conditions; learners classify each as physiological or behavioural. Use a 3-question concept check quiz by show of cards (A/B/C) at the end: for example, 'Which response lowers body temperature: vasoconstriction, vasodilation or shivering?' Record the number of correct answers to decide which ideas to revisit.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups build a concept map or flowchart of a negative feedback loop for body temperature, labelling stimulus (rise in body temperature), receptors (thermoreceptors in skin and hypothalamus), control centre (hypothalamus), effectors (sweat glands, skin arterioles, muscles) and response (sweating, vasodilation, panting) and then the reverse loop for cold (vasoconstriction, shivering, hair erection). They then add a branch for behavioural responses. Using their evidence, each group writes a 3 to 4 sentence explanation for the dog and the lizard: the dog (an endotherm) loses heat through panting, which evaporates water from the tongue and airways, and through vasodilation; the lizard (an ectotherm) cannot regulate heat internally and uses behaviour, so it basks to gain heat, then moves into shade or a crevice when too hot. Groups also match other local examples (burrowing by mole rats and termites, hibernation, aestivation in lungfish and some frogs and snails during dry spells in northern Kenya) to the problem each solves. Finally, learners link back to the goats and fish: water balance and temperature control both use feedback loops.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use your evidence to show how the loop works. Every arrow must be justified by something you observed.' Give 10 minutes to build the flowchart and 5 minutes to write the explanations. Circulate and ask: 'What happens next if the body is still too hot? How does the loop stop?' 'Why is this called negative feedback?' WAIT 10 to 15 seconds. Then run a gallery walk: groups swap charts and leave 1 sticky note with a question or suggestion. Cold-call 3 groups to explain the dog and 3 groups to explain the lizard, and ask the class to compare: 'What is the same and what is different?' Address any misconception that the dog sweats through its tongue, or that the lizard produces its own heat. Prompt: 'Why does panting also cause the dog to lose water? How might that link to what we learned about the goats and kidney function?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concept mapping/flowcharts of homeostatic feedback loops: laying out stimulus, receptor, control centre, effector and response turns separate facts into a causal chain and makes the idea of negative feedback visible. Peer review in the gallery walk helps learners test their reasoning against others and refine their explanations of the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer-reviewed flowcharts and written explanations. Observable indicators: all 5 loop components are present and ordered correctly; the cold loop shows vasoconstriction and shivering; the explanation names panting or vasodilation for the dog and basking, shade-seeking or burrowing for the lizard; learners note that ectotherms depend on the environment. Use a rubric of 'Complete / Partly complete / Not yet' for each criterion. Oral probes record whether learners can state why the loop is 'negative'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revisit the class Driving Question Board and the question 'How do different animals maintain a balanced internal environment and eliminate toxic wastes despite drastic changes in their external conditions?' Each group writes one answered question (for example, 'Why does the dog pant?') on a sticky note with a short evidence summary and moves it to the 'Answered' section. Each group also writes one new question (for example, 'What happens to the kidney and the body if an animal loses too much water through panting or sweating?' or 'Why do excretion and homeostasis matter for survival?') and adds it to the board. The class reads the new questions and sorts them into clusters such as water balance, temperature and survival.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our board. Which of our questions can we now answer, and what evidence do we have?' Give 3 minutes for groups to write, then WAIT 10 to 15 seconds as notes are placed. Cold-call 3 groups to read an answered question and justify it with evidence from today's stations. Ask: 'Which new questions connect temperature control with what we learned about the kidney and sweat?' Highlight the question about why excretion and homeostasis are vital for the overall survival of organisms and say: 'This will be our focus next lesson.' Praise questions that ask 'how' and 'why' rather than 'what'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board discussion: displaying answered and new questions makes learning progress visible and keeps learners' own questions steering the unit. Clustering links today's evidence to earlier lessons on urine formation and the skin, and gives purpose to the next investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Quality of sticky-note questions and evidence statements. Observable indicators: answered notes cite specific evidence (a diagram or field note); new questions link two ideas, such as water loss and kidney function; at least half the groups contribute a question that points to survival. The teacher notes patterns of misunderstanding to address in Lesson 7.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners revise their cumulative class or group model of how animals maintain a balanced internal environment and remove wastes. Using poster paper, they keep the earlier components (excretory organs, nephron and urine formation, liver and skin) and add a new thermoregulation section with a feedback loop and a panel for behavioural strategies. They use colours for new additions, label the dog and lizard, and add the goats and fish to show osmoregulation. In pairs, they swap models and give peer review using 2 stars (what is well represented) and a wish (what is missing or unclear). Finally, learners complete an exit ticket: (1) Draw or write the steps of the loop that cools a hot body; (2) Explain in two sentences why the lizard stays still on the hot rock while the dog pants; (3) Write one question about why excretion and homeostasis are vital for survival.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Add today's evidence to your model. Use a new colour for everything you add or change, and show how thermoregulation connects to water balance and waste removal.' Give 12 minutes. Circulate and ask: 'Where does the heat go when the dog pants? What does that cost the dog in water?' 'How would your model show the goat in the same heat?' WAIT 10 to 15 seconds after each question. Facilitate peer review with the prompt: 'Give two stars and a wish.' Cold-call 3 pairs to share one revision they made and why. Collect exit tickets at the door. Close by saying: 'If every system works to keep the body steady, what could happen when it fails? That is our question for next lesson.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model building and revision: adding thermoregulation to the evolving model lets learners integrate temperature control with excretion and osmoregulation into one coherent explanation of homeostasis. Colour-coded revisions make conceptual change visible, and peer review builds a shared standard for a good model.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer review of models and exit tickets. Observable indicators: the model shows a labelled feedback loop with sensor, control centre and effector; it separates physiological from behavioural responses; the dog and lizard are correctly explained; connections to water balance appear. On exit tickets, a successful response correctly orders the cooling steps (temperature rise detected, hypothalamus signals, vasodilation and sweating or panting, temperature falls) and contrasts endotherm with ectotherm. Sort tickets into 'secure', 'developing' and 'needs support' to plan reteaching.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Before the lesson, did I collect or prepare field notes, video clips and printed diagrams so that groups sharing one device still get equal access? After the lesson, which learners could explain the loop in their own words and which only copied labels? Did any hold the idea that the lizard is 'lazy' or that dogs sweat through their tongues, and did the evidence change their thinking? Were the cold-calls spread across the whole room? How well did learners connect temperature control to water balance and kidney function, and which students need support with negative feedback? What adjustments are needed to the DQB clusters to prepare for Lesson 7 on why excretion and homeostasis are vital for survival?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed a dog panting and cattle and goats resting in shade at midday, an agama lizard basking on a rock in the morning and moving into shade or a crevice at midday, and, in video clips and notes, animals that burrow, hibernate or aestivate during extreme cold or dry conditions. We also saw diagrams of blood vessels in the skin widening (vasodilation) and narrowing (vasoconstriction) and of sweating and shivering.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Body temperature is kept within a narrow range by negative feedback: thermoreceptors detect a change, the hypothalamus acts as control centre, and effectors such as sweat glands, skin arterioles and muscles reverse the change. Endotherms like dogs, goats and humans use physiological responses (sweating, panting, vasodilation, vasoconstriction, shivering) plus behaviour, while ectotherms like lizards rely mainly on behaviour (basking, shade-seeking, burrowing). Hibernation and aestivation help animals survive prolonged cold or hot, dry periods.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The dog pants because evaporation of water from its tongue and airways carries heat away, and its skin blood vessels dilate to lose heat, keeping its body temperature steady. The lizard stays still on the warm rock because it cannot control its temperature internally, so it gains heat by basking and moves into shade when it gets too hot. Both are using homeostasis to survive heat, which raises the question of why excretion and homeostasis are so vital for the survival of all living organisms.

LESSONS.title: Putting It All Together: Final Explanation of How Animals Keep a Balanced Internal Environment and Remove Toxic Wastes
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 3.3: Excretion and Homeostasis in Animals
LESSONS.aresKeywords: homeostasis, excretion, osmoregulation, thermoregulation, negative feedback, nephron, kidney, urea, ammonia, uric acid, panting, basking, final model, DQB

slo.purpose: Learners synthesise evidence from Lessons 1-6 into a final explanatory model that accounts for the anchoring phenomenon (panting dog, basking lizard, goats producing concentrated urine, freshwater fish producing dilute urine). They compare it with their Lesson 1 model and present answers to the Driving Question Board (DQB).
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (a) relate excretory structures and their products in insects, birds, freshwater and marine fish, and mammals; (b) relate the internal structure of the mammalian kidney (cortex, medulla, pelvis, nephron) to its function in urine formation; (c) relate the structure of the liver and skin to their excretory functions; (d) illustrate homeostatic regulation in humans (osmoregulation, thermoregulation, blood sugar regulation) using negative feedback; (e) reflect on the importance of excretion and homeostasis in animals.
slo.skills: Developing and using models (revising a cumulative model); Constructing explanations (claim-evidence-reasoning); Engaging in argument from evidence (peer review of models); Analysing and interpreting data (comparing Lesson 1 and final models); Obtaining, evaluating and communicating information (presenting DQB answers); Asking questions to be clear on what is needed (Critical Thinking and Problem Solving).
slo.attitudes: Responsibility: engaging in assigned roles and duties during group work and presentations. Social Justice: sharing resources (devices, specimens, charts) equitably. Environmental Conservation and Waste Management: appreciating the need to conserve biodiversity by recognising how local animals respond to environmental changes. Observing laboratory safety when handling kidney specimens.
slo.keyInquiry: 1. How do animals get rid of waste products? 2. How do animals cope with environmental changes? Driving Question: How do different animals maintain a balanced internal environment and eliminate toxic wastes despite drastic changes in their external conditions?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the final lesson of the unit. Learners have gathered evidence on excretion in insects, birds and fish, kidney structure and dissection, urine formation, liver and skin, human homeostasis (osmoregulation, thermoregulation, blood sugar regulation, diabetes mellitus and insipidus), liver disorders and animal behavioural responses (basking, panting, hibernation, burrowing, aestivation). Now they unify it into one explanation of the phenomenon. Core idea: keeping a constant internal environment (homeostasis) and clearing metabolic waste (excretion) are essential for cellular survival and overall health. This is a unit reflection, so no new question is raised.
slo.safetyNotes: Any kidney specimens revisited for the Predict-Observe-Explain check must be fresh goat or cow kidney from a local butcher, handled with gloves, on trays, with scalpels used only by the assigned group member. Wash hands with soap and water after handling. Dispose of specimens by burying in a pit or as the school directs. Keep food and drink away from specimens. Limit digital devices to group viewing, with cables and chargers kept off walkways.

LESSONS.overview: Learners return to the hot-afternoon scene: a panting dog, a still lizard on a warm rock, goats making concentrated urine and freshwater fish making large volumes of dilute urine. Over two periods they (1) predict, then check, how a kidney and feedback loop explain these differences, (2) build a final model with claim-evidence-reasoning statements, (3) compare it with their Lesson 1 model, (4) close the DQB by presenting answers to every question, and (5) reflect on why excretion and homeostasis matter for cell survival and health. Large classes work in groups of 5-6 with one shared device and one kidney or diagram set per group. Teacher walks the room with the rubric sheet.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the phenomenon image or the teacher's re-telling of the scene (dog, lizard, goat, tilapia from Lake Victoria). Individually they write a 2-minute prediction: 'If a goat is deprived of water for a day on a hot afternoon in Kajiado, what will happen to (a) its urine concentration, (b) its body temperature, (c) its blood water level, and which organ and hormone are involved?' They then Think-Pair-Share with a partner and add one sentence connecting their prediction to the lizard or the fish.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the phenomenon image and say: 'Remember the dog, the lizard, the goat and the fish? Today you will explain them using everything we have learned.' Read the prompt aloud. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds of silent thinking before writing. Circulate and note 3 predictions to share. Say: 'Turn to your partner and explain WHY, not just WHAT.' Cold-call 4 pairs, asking: 'What did your partner say that you had not thought of?' Record the predictions on the board under 'Predictions to test'. Do not correct yet.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share combined with the Predict step of Predict-Observe-Explain. Committing to a prediction makes learners aware of their current ideas, so that the later evidence check shows how their thinking has changed. Pairing exposes alternative ideas such as 'goats just drink less' versus 'the kidney conserves water through ADH'.
framework.formativeAssessment: Oral probes and prediction sheets. Indicators: learner mentions kidney or nephron and water reabsorption for the goat; links high temperature to sweating, panting or behaviour; uses the word 'balance' or 'constant'; notes common misconceptions (e.g. 'fish do not need to excrete because they live in water'). Teacher tallies how many of the 4 cold-called pairs mention a hormone or feedback.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 5-6 review their evidence set: (1) the labelled kidney and nephron drawings from the dissection, (2) the urine-formation animation, watched again in groups on one shared device for 3 minutes, (3) the feedback-loop charts for thermoregulation, osmoregulation and blood sugar, and (4) the comparison table of nitrogenous wastes (ammonia in freshwater fish, urea in mammals, uric acid in insects and birds). Using a fresh goat or cow kidney from the local butchery, if available, each group does a quick Predict-Observe-Explain check: predict where the cortex, medulla and pelvis will be on a cut surface, locate them, and explain how each relates to filtration, concentration of urine and collection. Each group fills the evidence table: Animal | Environmental challenge | Waste product | Organ or behaviour | How it keeps balance.
framework.teacherMoves: Assign roles (specimen handler, recorder, device operator, reporter, safety monitor) and say: 'Everyone has a role, and roles rotate so that resources are shared fairly.' Review the safety rules before gloves go on. Give 2 minutes of WAIT TIME for groups to predict the layers of the kidney before they observe. Circulate with the rubric and ask: 'Which part of this kidney makes sure the goat loses little water?' and 'Why does the fish lose so much water, and which part of its body is losing it?' Cold-call 3 reporters to state one observation each. Pause the animation at the loop of Henle and ask: 'What is happening to water here?' Wait 10 seconds before taking answers.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain on the kidney specimen, plus an evidence table. Learners test their mental model against real tissue and tie structure to function. The table forces them to compare across animals (insects, birds, fish, mammals) so patterns emerge: the waste product and the strategy depend on the water available and the energy cost.
framework.formativeAssessment: Annotated kidney/nephron diagrams and oral probes. Indicators: correct labelling of cortex, medulla, pelvis, glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, loop of Henle and collecting duct; correctly states that the glomerulus filters and the tubule reabsorbs; evidence table has at least 4 animals correctly matched to waste product and strategy; safe handling observed (gloves, trays, hand washing). Teacher ticks a checklist for each group.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group writes a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) explanation for the four animals in the phenomenon. Example claim: 'Different animals keep a stable internal environment using structures and behaviours suited to their habitat.' Evidence is cited from the lessons (e.g. panting increases evaporation to cool the dog; basking lets the ectothermic lizard raise its body temperature, and it moves to shade when too hot; the goat's long loops of Henle and ADH produce concentrated urine; the freshwater fish gains water by osmosis and excretes large volumes of dilute urine). Groups then draw a concept map or flowchart of a negative feedback loop (stimulus → receptor → control centre → effector → response → return to set point) for one example: thermoregulation in the dog, blood sugar regulation (insulin/glucagon, linking to diabetes mellitus) or osmoregulation (ADH, linking to diabetes insipidus). They add the liver (deamination, urea formation) and skin (sweat) to show where wastes come from and leave.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your explanation must answer WHY the dog pants, WHY the lizard stays still, and WHY the goat and the fish differ.' Provide the CER frame on the board. Allow 10-15 seconds of WAIT TIME after each question before calling on anyone. Prompt: 'What would happen to the loop if the effector stopped working? Which disorder have we studied that fits?' Cold-call 5 learners from different groups to share one link in their feedback loop and ask each: 'What is your evidence?' Invite a different group to challenge: 'Do you agree? Why or why not?' Address misconceptions, e.g. that lizards 'do not control' temperature (they do so behaviourally), or that panting 'makes the dog lose waste' (it mainly loses heat by evaporation).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concept Mapping/Flowcharts of homeostatic feedback loops, plus CER. Drawing the loop makes causal chains visible and shows that homeostasis in all examples follows the same logic, while CER links claims to evidence. This moves learners from lists of facts to mechanisms.
framework.formativeAssessment: Concept check quiz (5 questions, 5 minutes, done individually) and oral probes. Indicators: CER has a claim, at least two pieces of evidence and reasoning that mentions negative feedback; flowchart has all six components in correct order and the arrows show reversal back toward the set point; learner correctly distinguishes ectotherm behaviour from endotherm physiology; at least 4 of 5 quiz items are correct. Teacher records learners scoring below 3 for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners go to the class DQB wall. Each group takes 3-4 sticky notes of questions from earlier lessons (e.g. 'Why does the lizard bask?', 'Why do fish urinate so much?', 'What happens if the liver fails?', 'Why do diabetics pass a lot of urine?'). They write an answer on a new note with evidence, place it next to the question, and mark each question as Answered, Partly answered or New. Groups present 2 answers to the class in 90 seconds each, using their model. The class identifies remaining questions as areas for further study (such as local liver disease and community health or conservation of local wildlife during drought), without launching a new unit.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our DQB is not finished until each question has an answer backed by evidence.' Give each group a colour of marker. Before presentations, allow 10-15 seconds of WAIT TIME for groups to rehearse silently. During presentations ask the audience: 'What evidence supports that answer?' Cold-call 3 learners from other groups to paraphrase an answer. Use the rubric sheet to score presentations. Point out that answers link to both KICD key inquiry questions: waste removal and coping with environmental change. Close with: 'Which question taught you the most?' and take 3 volunteers.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board discussion. Revisiting learner-generated questions shows that the unit was driven by their curiosity, and presenting evidence-based answers consolidates learning through explanation. Marking questions Answered/Partly/New builds metacognition about what they know.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer review and oral probes using the rubric. Indicators: each answer cites at least one piece of evidence from the unit; presenters use correct terms (osmoregulation, reabsorption, negative feedback, deamination); audience members accurately paraphrase; at least 80% of DQB questions are marked Answered or Partly answered with justification. Teacher notes unresolved misconceptions.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups take out the Lesson 1 initial model (their first drawing of how the dog, lizard, goat and fish cope). On a large sheet they draw the Final Model showing: (1) external changes (heat, water availability, salinity), (2) sensors and control (brain, hormones such as ADH, insulin), (3) organs for excretion (kidney, liver, skin, gills, Malpighian tubules), (4) wastes (ammonia, urea, uric acid, CO2), (5) behaviours (basking, panting, burrowing, hibernation, aestivation), and (6) the outcome: stable internal conditions that keep cells alive. They use a different colour for the changes from Lesson 1 and write 'I used to think... Now I think... because...'. Groups swap models for a gallery walk and peer review with two stars and a wish. Finally, individually, learners complete the exit ticket and the summary table (below), reflecting on why excretion and homeostasis matter, for example how kidney failure or liver disease affects a person's health in their community.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your final model must explain all four animals, not just one.' Display success criteria: includes cause-and-effect arrows, all three wastes, one feedback loop, and at least two behaviours. Give 10-15 seconds of WAIT TIME before groups begin drawing so they plan. Circulate and ask: 'Where on your model is the goat's water saved?' and 'Where does the fish lose water balance, and how does it fix it?' During the gallery walk, stand at the exit and cold-call 4 learners: 'Name one change you made from your first model and the evidence that made you change it.' Collect exit tickets. Conclude: 'Excretion and homeostasis keep every cell alive; when they fail, health suffers.' Do not introduce a new question; this is the unit reflection.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model Building and Revision with Lesson 1 versus final comparison. Putting earlier and final models side by side makes conceptual change visible and shows the learner how evidence has improved their explanation. Peer review through the gallery walk develops argumentation skills.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer review of physical models, exit tickets and the rubric. Indicators: final model includes all six elements and explains each of the four animals; at least three specific revisions from Lesson 1 are labelled with reasons; peer feedback is specific (two stars and a wish); exit ticket states one way excretion protects cells and one way homeostasis protects health, using correct vocabulary. Proficiency: 4 of 5 rubric criteria met.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: Did learners explain all four animals with the same underlying principles (balance of water, temperature and wastes via feedback), or only recall isolated facts? Which groups still confuse ectothermic behaviour with endothermic physiology, or ammonia/urea/uric acid with habitat? Were devices and kidney specimens shared fairly in large groups, and did every learner have a real role? Which DQB questions remain Partly answered and why? Compare Lesson 1 and final models for 5 learners to judge growth, and plan remedial support (for example, a short revision on the nephron) for those who scored below the proficiency threshold. Note any safety lapses during the specimen check and how the next class can avoid them.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What we observed: the panting dog, the basking lizard, goats producing concentrated urine and freshwater fish producing large volumes of dilute urine; the layers of the goat or cow kidney (cortex, medulla, pelvis); wastes in insects, birds, fish and mammals; and how feedback loops work.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What we learned: homeostasis keeps temperature, water, salts and blood sugar steady using negative feedback; excretion removes toxic metabolic wastes such as ammonia, urea and uric acid; the kidney, liver and skin do this work in mammals; and behaviours such as basking, panting, burrowing, hibernation and aestivation help animals cope with environmental change.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Our final explanation: Animals face different environments, but all must keep their cells in a stable internal environment and remove toxic wastes. The dog pants to lose heat; the lizard basks or shelters to adjust its temperature behaviourally; the goat's nephrons reabsorb water to make concentrated urine; the freshwater fish gains water by osmosis and excretes dilute urine. Because each structure or behaviour suits the animal's habitat, its cells survive and it stays healthy. This is why excretion and homeostasis are essential.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Biology Grade 11: Excretion and Homeostasis in Animals
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: Welcome to your Final Explanation. Think back to the hot afternoon in a Kenyan community: a dog pants with its tongue out, a lizard sits still on a warm rock, goats drink water yet make concentrated urine, and freshwater fish keep excreting large amounts of dilute urine. Use everything you observed and learned in Lessons 1 to 7 to answer the questions below. Write your answers in the space under each question. Use evidence from your kidney dissection, your charts, your 'Follow the Fluid' table, your feedback flowcharts and your class model. Use correct terms such as nitrogenous waste, ultrafiltration, reabsorption, ADH, negative feedback, endotherm and ectotherm. Where a question asks for a claim, evidence and reasoning, state your claim first, support it with evidence, then explain why the evidence supports it. Your last task is to plan the annotated poster that will be your final product.

sections.title: Part 1: Getting rid of nitrogenous wastes in different habitats
sections.prompt: Animals make toxic nitrogenous wastes when they break down proteins. (a) Name the three nitrogenous wastes you studied and say which animals you linked to each one: freshwater fish, marine fish, insects, birds and mammals. (b) Explain how the type of waste an animal makes is linked to how much water is available to it. Use the freshwater fish and the insects and birds in your explanation. (c) Name the excretory structures used by freshwater fish, marine fish, insects and birds.
sections.exemplar: (a) The three wastes are ammonia, urea and uric acid. Freshwater fish excrete ammonia. Marine cartilaginous fish (such as sharks) and mammals make urea. Insects and birds make uric acid. (b) The type of waste is linked to water availability. Freshwater fish have plenty of water available, and they excrete toxic ammonia in dilute urine. Insects and birds must save water, and they excrete less toxic uric acid as a semi-solid paste. (c) Freshwater fish and marine fish use gills and kidneys. Insects use Malpighian tubules. Birds use kidneys. In each case the structure removes nitrogenous waste in a way that suits the water available to the animal.

sections.title: Part 2: How the mammalian kidney makes urine
sections.prompt: Think about the goat kidney you dissected and the animations of the nephron. (a) Describe what you saw in the cortex, medulla and pelvis, and say what each region does. (b) Using your 'Follow the Fluid' table, explain the steps by which blood becomes urine. Include ultrafiltration, selective reabsorption and secretion. (c) Explain why glucose is found in blood and filtrate but not in urine, while urea is more concentrated in urine. (d) Which hormone controls how much water is reabsorbed, and where in the nephron does it act?
sections.exemplar: (a) The cortex was the dark outer region with granular dots; it contains many nephrons where blood is filtered. The medulla was paler and striped; it contains parts of the nephrons and collecting ducts that help concentrate urine. The pelvis was a hollow space that collects urine and passes it to the ureter. Blood vessels (renal artery and vein) entered and left at the hilum, showing a large blood supply. The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney. (b) In the glomerulus, blood is under high pressure, so small molecules (water, glucose, urea, salts) are forced into Bowman's capsule. This is ultrafiltration. Blood cells and proteins are too large and stay in the blood. As the filtrate moves along the tubule, useful substances are selectively reabsorbed into the blood, and extra wastes and ions are secreted into the tubule. The remaining fluid is urine. It passes through the collecting duct to the pelvis, ureter and bladder. (c) All glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, so none is left in urine. Water is reabsorbed in the loop of Henle and collecting duct, so the volume of fluid falls and urea becomes more concentrated in the urine. (d) ADH controls how much water is reabsorbed. It acts on the collecting duct, so urine can be concentrated or dilute.

sections.title: Part 3: The liver and skin, and the goat and the freshwater fish
sections.prompt: (a) Where does the urea in a goat's urine come from, and how does it reach the urine? (b) State one other job of the liver and one job of the skin in excretion. (c) Explain why a goat that has lost water on a hot day makes small amounts of concentrated urine, while a freshwater fish makes large amounts of dilute urine. Write this as a claim, evidence and reasoning explanation, using what you learned about the kidney for the goat and about water movement for the fish.
sections.exemplar: (a) The urea starts in the liver, where excess amino acids are deaminated to make urea. Blood carries the urea to the kidney, where it is filtered at the glomerulus and removed in the urine. (b) The liver also breaks down haemoglobin to make bile pigments and processes toxic substances. The skin excretes sweat containing water, salts and a little urea, and sweat helps cool the body. (c) Claim: The goat conserves water by making concentrated urine, while the freshwater fish gets rid of extra water by making dilute urine. Evidence: In our Follow the Fluid table, urine became concentrated when water was reabsorbed in the loop of Henle and collecting duct. Freshwater fish gain water by osmosis and excrete large amounts of dilute urine. Reasoning: A goat that loses water on a hot day releases more ADH. ADH makes the collecting ducts reabsorb more water back into the blood, so little water is left in the urine, which is concentrated. The freshwater fish takes in water by osmosis from its surroundings, so it must remove the excess and does not need to save water, so its urine is dilute and plentiful. Both are controlling water balance to keep the internal environment stable.

sections.title: Part 4: Negative feedback and the dog and the lizard
sections.prompt: (a) Explain what negative feedback means, using a set point. (b) Draw or describe a feedback loop for either blood glucose after a meal of ugali and sukuma wiki, or body temperature on a hot day. Name the detector, the control centre and the effectors or hormones. (c) Explain why the dog pants and why the lizard sits still on the warm rock. In your answer, use the words endotherm and ectotherm. (d) Name two behaviours, other than basking and seeking shade, that animals use to survive extreme cold or dry conditions.
sections.exemplar: (a) Negative feedback detects a change away from a set point and triggers a response that reverses the change, bringing the body back to normal. (b) Temperature on a hot day: thermoreceptors detect that the body is too warm. The hypothalamus is the control centre. Effectors respond: sweat glands release sweat, skin arterioles widen (vasodilation) so more heat is lost, and panting increases. Body temperature falls back to the set point and the response slows. (Blood glucose alternative: after a meal glucose rises, the pancreas releases insulin, glucose levels fall; if glucose falls too low, glucagon is released to raise it.) (c) The dog is an endotherm. It pants so that water evaporates from its tongue and airways and carries heat away, and its skin blood vessels dilate to lose heat, so its body temperature stays steady. The lizard is an ectotherm. It cannot control its temperature internally, so it relies on behaviour: it gains heat by basking on the warm rock and moves into shade or a crevice when it gets too hot. Both are using homeostasis to survive the heat. (d) Any two of: burrowing, hibernation, aestivation. These help animals survive prolonged cold or hot, dry periods.

sections.title: Part 5: Your final poster and why homeostasis matters
sections.prompt: Your final product is an annotated poster model explaining how a mammal (a goat or a human) regulates its internal environment and excretes waste. (a) List at least five labelled parts or processes your poster must include and say what each shows. (b) Explain how your poster model is different from your first model in Lesson 1. (c) Explain why excretion and homeostasis are essential for the survival of the cells and health of all living organisms.
sections.exemplar: (a) Possible poster parts: 1) the kidney with cortex, medulla and pelvis, showing where filtering and urine concentration happen; 2) a nephron showing ultrafiltration at the glomerulus, selective reabsorption and secretion; 3) the liver, showing deamination to make urea and bile production; 4) the skin, showing sweat glands and the loss of water, salts and a little urea; 5) feedback loops: ADH for water balance, insulin and glucagon for blood glucose, and a temperature loop using the hypothalamus, vasodilation, vasoconstriction, sweating and shivering. Each part should have a label and a one-sentence note on its function, linked to the hot afternoon puzzle. (b) My Lesson 1 model only showed that animals have different wastes and could not explain panting, basking or concentrated urine. My final model adds the kidney structure, nephron processes, the liver and skin, and negative feedback control, so it explains how the goat makes concentrated urine, why the dog pants, and why the lizard basks. (c) Cells only work properly in a stable internal environment with steady temperature, water, salts and blood sugar. Toxic wastes such as ammonia and urea would build up and damage cells if they were not removed. Excretion and homeostasis prevent this, so animals in different habitats survive and stay healthy despite changes in the environment.

SUMMARY_TABLE.subStrand: Sub-Strand 3.3: Excretion and Homeostasis in Animals
SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: How do different animals maintain a balanced internal environment and eliminate toxic wastes despite drastic changes in their external conditions?

lessons.title: Same Hot Afternoon, Different Bodies: Launching the Excretion and Homeostasis Puzzle
lessons.observed: We observed that freshwater fish, marine fish, insects and birds have different excretory structures (gills and kidneys, Malpighian tubules, kidneys) and make different nitrogenous wastes (ammonia, urea, uric acid), and that a dog pants, a lizard sits still on a hot rock, goats produce concentrated urine and freshwater fish produce large amounts of dilute urine.
lessons.learned: We learned that the type of nitrogenous waste an animal makes is linked to how much water is available to it: animals with plenty of water (freshwater fish) excrete toxic ammonia in dilute urine, while animals that must save water (insects and birds) excrete less toxic uric acid as a semi-solid paste, and marine cartilaginous fish (such as sharks) and mammals make urea.
lessons.explained: We can explain that animals living in different environments have excretory structures adapted to remove nitrogenous wastes while conserving or removing water, but we cannot yet explain how a goat makes concentrated urine, why a dog pants, why a lizard basks, or how mammals such as humans filter their internal liquid wastes. That leads us to ask: How do mammals (like humans) process and filter their internal liquid wastes?

lessons.title: Inside the Goat Kidney: Cortex, Medulla, Pelvis and Nephrons
lessons.observed: We observed a goat/cow kidney with a dark outer cortex, a paler striped medulla, a hollow renal pelvis leading to the ureter, and blood vessels (renal artery and vein) entering and leaving at the hilum. Granular dots in the cortex suggested tiny filtering units.
lessons.learned: The mammalian kidney is organised into regions with different roles: the cortex contains many nephrons where blood is filtered, the medulla contains parts of nephrons and collecting ducts that help concentrate urine, and the pelvis collects urine and passes it to the ureter. The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
lessons.explained: Because the kidney receives a large blood supply and contains millions of nephrons arranged in the cortex and medulla, it can filter blood, remove urea and regulate water. This helps explain how a goat can drink water yet produce concentrated urine, while we still need to find out how nephrons turn filtered blood into urine and why freshwater fish produce dilute urine.

lessons.title: Following the Fluid: How the Nephron Filters Blood and Makes Urine
lessons.observed: We watched animations of the nephron and traced how blood, filtrate and urine differ in glucose, protein, urea and water. We saw that blood cells and proteins stay in the blood, glucose is fully reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, and urine is concentrated by water reabsorption in the loop of Henle and collecting duct.
lessons.learned: Urine formation involves ultrafiltration in the glomerulus (small molecules forced into Bowman's capsule under high pressure), followed by selective reabsorption of useful substances and secretion of extra wastes and ions in the nephron tubule. ADH controls how much water is reabsorbed, so urine can be concentrated or dilute.
lessons.explained: A goat that loses water on a hot day releases more ADH, so its collecting ducts reabsorb more water and it produces small amounts of concentrated urine. A freshwater fish gains water by osmosis, so it produces large amounts of dilute urine. New question: What other organs in mammals assist in excretion besides the kidney?

lessons.title: Liver and Skin: Hidden Waste Processors Behind the Hot Afternoon
lessons.observed: We observed photomicrographs and charts of the liver (hepatocytes, sinusoids, bile canaliculi) and skin (epidermis, dermis, sweat glands, capillaries), and heard about cirrhosis, hepatitis and fatty liver disease.
lessons.learned: The liver deaminates excess amino acids to make urea, breaks down haemoglobin to make bile pigments and processes toxic substances; the skin excretes sweat containing water, salts and a little urea and helps cool the body. Liver disorders damage these functions.
lessons.explained: Urea in the goat's urine begins in the liver, is carried by blood to the kidney and removed, while sweat or panting helps animals lose heat on a hot afternoon. The liver and skin work with the kidney to remove wastes and keep the body stable, but we still need to explain how water, temperature and sugar levels are kept constant.

lessons.title: Feedback Loops: How the Body Keeps Water and Blood Glucose Steady
lessons.observed: We observed that hormone signals such as ADH, insulin and glucagon form feedback loops, and that in diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus the symptoms (thirst, lots of urine, sugar in urine or very dilute urine) show where a loop has failed.
lessons.learned: We learned that negative feedback detects a change from a set point and triggers a response that reverses it; ADH adjusts how much water the kidney reabsorbs, and insulin and glucagon keep blood glucose within a narrow range.
lessons.explained: We can explain why the goat can produce concentrated urine to save water while the freshwater fish excretes dilute urine, how the body keeps water and glucose steady after exercise and a meal, and why the next question is how body temperature is kept stable in animals like the dog and the lizard.

lessons.title: Keeping Cool and Staying Warm: Thermoregulation in the Dog, the Lizard and Us
lessons.observed: We observed a dog panting and cattle and goats resting in shade at midday, an agama lizard basking on a rock in the morning and moving into shade or a crevice at midday, and, in video clips and notes, animals that burrow, hibernate or aestivate during extreme cold or dry conditions. We also saw diagrams of blood vessels in the skin widening (vasodilation) and narrowing (vasoconstriction) and of sweating and shivering.
lessons.learned: Body temperature is kept within a narrow range by negative feedback: thermoreceptors detect a change, the hypothalamus acts as control centre, and effectors such as sweat glands, skin arterioles and muscles reverse the change. Endotherms like dogs, goats and humans use physiological responses (sweating, panting, vasodilation, vasoconstriction, shivering) plus behaviour, while ectotherms like lizards rely mainly on behaviour (basking, shade-seeking, burrowing). Hibernation and aestivation help animals survive prolonged cold or hot, dry periods.
lessons.explained: The dog pants because evaporation of water from its tongue and airways carries heat away, and its skin blood vessels dilate to lose heat, keeping its body temperature steady. The lizard stays still on the warm rock because it cannot control its temperature internally, so it gains heat by basking and moves into shade when it gets too hot. Both are using homeostasis to survive heat, which raises the question of why excretion and homeostasis are so vital for the survival of all living organisms.

lessons.title: Putting It All Together: Final Explanation of How Animals Keep a Balanced Internal Environment and Remove Toxic Wastes
lessons.observed: What we observed: the panting dog, the basking lizard, goats producing concentrated urine and freshwater fish producing large volumes of dilute urine; the layers of the goat or cow kidney (cortex, medulla, pelvis); wastes in insects, birds, fish and mammals; and how feedback loops work.
lessons.learned: What we learned: homeostasis keeps temperature, water, salts and blood sugar steady using negative feedback; excretion removes toxic metabolic wastes such as ammonia, urea and uric acid; the kidney, liver and skin do this work in mammals; and behaviours such as basking, panting, burrowing, hibernation and aestivation help animals cope with environmental change.
lessons.explained: Our final explanation: Animals face different environments, but all must keep their cells in a stable internal environment and remove toxic wastes. The dog pants to lose heat; the lizard basks or shelters to adjust its temperature behaviourally; the goat's nephrons reabsorb water to make concentrated urine; the freshwater fish gains water by osmosis and excretes dilute urine. Because each structure or behaviour suits the animal's habitat, its cells survive and it stays healthy. This is why excretion and homeostasis are essential.
